news.title: ​Jensen Huang Weighs Return as Nvidia CEO Amid Silicon Valley Lobbying Push; US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent Demands Leadership Shake-Up
news.text:
The push to bring back Nvidia’s 63-year-old co-founder has gained rapid momentum over the weekend, setting up a sharp clash between Silicon Valley backers—who warn of leadership uncertainty—and senior policymakers in Washington demanding stricter oversight over US chip export controls.

​Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney & Investors Rally Behind ‘Bring Jensen Back’ Push

​While CFO Colette Kress continues to serve as interim CEO, an organized group of technology executives and institutional shareholders has urged Nvidia’s board not to rush into replacing Huang:

​Tech Leaders & Open Letter Support: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney—alongside Y Combinator’s Garry Tan—are among high-profile figures backing a petition and open letter urging Nvidia’s board to “Bring Jensen Back,” an online campaign that has already gathered over 160,000 signatures.
​Institutional Investors Urge Caution: In a public letter shared on X late last week, Altimeter Capital Management’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker praised “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and called on the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach that explicitly includes considering Huang’s possible return.

​Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent Pushes Back, Demands Export Compliance Answers

​Any comeback bid faces stiff headwinds from Washington. Appearing on Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang’s exit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shake-up” in Nvidia’s leadership—suggesting the board look outside the company for its next CEO—and shifted focus toward national security and trade compliance:

​10-Day Deadline on China Export Controls: Bessent pressed Nvidia to clarify within the next 10 days whether it knowingly allowed shell companies to circumvent US export restrictions to supply China with its most advanced AI processors, alongside sharing findings from its internal investigation into Huang’s conduct. While President Donald Trump authorized sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China in late 2025, top-tier AI processors remained strictly barred.

​”What’s more important here is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.”
— Scott Bessent, US Treasury Secretary

news.title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders Weighs 2028 Bid, Admits Dad May Not Support It
news.text: Republican Governor of Arkansas Sarah Huckabee Sanders has not ruled out a 2028 presidential bid. Speaking with CNN’s State of the Union Sunday, Sanders admitted that her father, Mike Huckabee, who served as the 44th Governor of Arkansas and had two Presidential bids, may not be keen on her throwing herself into the 2028 race. CNN Host Dana Bash asked Sanders if her dad would like to see her launch her own bid for the White House. She laughed as she responded: "I don't know. Given the fact that he knows what that means, I'm not sure he would wish that on me in some cases. But he ran, as you know, a - just a bootstrap campaign in 2008, came from behind, a victory that really changed the course of his adult life after that in a significant way and gave him a major platform to talk about issues he cared about." Huckabee, who is currently serving as United States Ambassador to Israel, was governor of Arkansas from 1996 to 2007 and launched campaigns for the U.S. presidency in 2008 and 2016. Newsweek has reached out to him for further comment. Sanders, 44, who became the first woman ever elected Arkansas governor in 2022, won reelection for a second term, securing 53.9 per cent of the vote in the midterms. Sanders continued: "For me personally, I just got reelected as the governor of Arkansas. I love what I'm doing. And I look forward to holding this job for the next four years. And my plan is to focus and do as best as I can lifting up the people of my state, moving my state forward, and really just keep my focus there for right now." Bash pressed Sanders on whether she was committing to serve the full four-year term. Sanders responded that she would be term-limited at that point, adding, "unless they change the rules," and saying her "max-out is in four years." The exchange came as some supporters and donors have reportedly encouraged Sanders to consider a presidential run. A spokesperson for the governor told ABC News that Sanders "looks forward to serving the people of Arkansas for the next four years." Before becoming governor, Sanders served as President Donald Trump's Press Secretary from July 2017 to June 2019. She was also a senior adviser to Trump's 2016 presidential campaign. Just a week after securing the midterm win, she released her memoir Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy on November 10. Fighting For Conservative Values Sanders touts the book as "a candid, no-nonsense account of fighting for conservative values, taking on the status quo, and laying out her bold vision for the future," according to the blurb shared by her publisher, Macmillan. "She traces her historic campaign, pulling back the curtain on the defining moments of her life - including a personal battle with cancer that unfolded just 60 days before her historic election - and the faith that sustains her," it added. In the book, she speaks about how she based her campaign on issues that matter most to Arkansans: education, lower taxes, jobs, and public safety. She told Bash: "I love what I'm doing. I'm focused on doing a really good job in the role that I have been elected to serve in right now. And that's the - the only race I cared about was the one that took place last week. And that's where I'm going to continue to lean in and continue to keep my focus." Pence Calls For A Competitive Primary Sanders' comments came as former Vice President Mike Pence called for a competitive Republican presidential primary in 2028. Appearing on NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Pence declined to endorse the idea that Vice President JD Vance is the presumptive frontrunner for the next GOP nomination, instead urging a debate over the party's ideological direction. Pence said the party must return to traditional conservative principles to recover from the sweeping midterm election losses that cost the GOP control of Congress. "I'm not a political pundit. I'll leave that speculation to others. But I would hope that we have a very vigorous debate going forward about the leadership of the party,” Pence, who was President Donald Trump's vice president in his first administration, told moderator Kristen Welker. Vance has not confirmed whether he will seek the presidency. At a CBS News town hall in Michigan prior to the midterms, he acknowledged there was "a chance" he would not run, citing his family and four young children. The 2028 Republican primary field remains unsettled. Earlier this month, Trump said in a 60 Minutes interview that he may stay out of the primary and refrain from endorsing a successor. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vance have long been seen as the two front-runners to succeed Trump in 2028. When asked by a reporter last week whether he still stood by his past promise to be the first to support Vance if he ran for president, Rubio said: "I'm not going to discuss 2028. I'm not going to discuss it in any form or fashion." A reporter tried 2032 instead. "Not even," Rubio said, laughing.
news.summary: Sarah Huckabee Sanders did not rule out a potential 2028 run for the White House and revealed what her father may think of it.

news.title: PM Modi, Trump to attend Quad leaders' meeting in Manila tomorrow
news.text: Leaders of the Quad countries — India, the United States, Australia and Japan — are scheduled to meet in Manila on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit, news agency PTI reported, citing a senior US official.The meeting, the first among Quad leaders in two years, will bring together Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.The previous Quad leaders' meeting was chaired by then US President Joe Biden in Delaware on September 21, 2024.Olivia Wales, Assistant Press Secretary at the White House, said that Trump would participate in the meeting on Tuesday, November 17, evening."The president will participate in a multilateral meeting with Quad leaders to discuss shared interests of peace, prosperity, and security in the Indo-Pacific region," she said.Wales said that under Trump's leadership, the Quad had demonstrated that it was a partnership focused on action, addressing the region's toughest challenges and creating opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific.The Quad was formed in 2007 but became largely inactive the following year amid concerns about provoking China.Trump revived the grouping in 2017 to address growing concerns over China's increasing economic, diplomatic and military influence in the Indo-Pacific, though he did not hold a leaders' summit during his earlier term.The Manila meeting will be the first Quad leaders' meeting during his current term as US President. Foreign ministers of the four countries have met five times since Trump began his second term on January 20, 2025.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had indicated last month that the Quad leaders could meet on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila. The Philippines is hosting the summit as the current chair of the 11-member ASEAN.- Ends(With PTI inputs)

news.title: Xi, Trump, Putin to hold first-ever trilateral meet on Nov 19
news.text: Beijing The first-ever trilateral meeting between the presidents of China, the US and Russia will be held on November 19, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said on Monday. Chinese President Xi Jinping will host Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. China is set to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18-19, with leaders of the 21-member grouping attending. The meeting would mark the first time the presidents of the three powerful countries have held a trilateral summit. Discussions at the meeting are expected to focus on a range of global issues, including conflicts, artificial intelligence and nuclear arms reduction. The proposed discussion on nuclear weapons comes amid concerns over the future of global arms control following the expiry of the New START treaty between the US and Russia in February. The last remaining major bilateral nuclear arms control agreement between the two countries, the New START treaty imposed legally binding limits on their strategic nuclear arsenals. Its expiry has left the world's two largest nuclear powers without such binding limits. "The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told the media last week. Beijing has shown little enthusiasm for trilateral nuclear arms control, citing its far smaller arsenal than those of Washington and Moscow, and has repeatedly stressed that it does not subscribe to a model of great power co-governance in global affairs. The Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post reported that the discussions could also explore possible commitments on regulating the use of artificial intelligence in nuclear arsenals as part of a broader global governance agenda. The three countries had engaged in weeks of discussions to finalise the agenda and protocol for the talks, the report said. Iran is another potential subject of discussion at the trilateral meeting. China is Iran's largest trading partner and the biggest buyer of its crude oil, giving Beijing a significant economic stake in the conflict involving Tehran. A senior US official said the war in Ukraine would not figure in the trilateral discussions, as Washington was pursuing a separate negotiating track with Moscow on the conflict. Russia has shown reluctance to discuss its war in Ukraine, the newspaper reported on Monday.
news.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping will host Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit

news.title: Shenzhen deploys additional police forces ahead of APEC summit
news.text:
SHENZHEN /China/, November 16. /TASS/. Additional police units have been deployed to the Chinese city of Shenzhen from across the Guangdong Province ahead of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, the Municipal Public Security Bureau said in a statement.

"All provincial public security agencies must organize their work at a high level, increase the number of deployed police officers and ensure strict control and a visible police presence on city streets," the statement reads. "Addiational police forces have been deployed to Shenzhen, with units from across the province engaged to ensure effective operations," the bureau added.

Police patrols have been stepped up across the city ahead of the summit, with authorities taking measures to prevent offences. Control over the transportation and storage of dangerous and explosive substances has been tightened. A ban on flights by drones and other low-altitude aerial vehicles has been imposed for the duration of the summit.

In early November, the Shenzhen government introduced a ban on the use of car signals for purposes unrelated to road safety.

Shenzhen will host the 33rd informal meeting of APEC leaders on November 18-19. The Russian delegation will be led by President Vladimir Putin, who is also expected to hold a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the summit. In addition, an agreement has been reached to hold a trilateral meeting between Putin, Xi and US President Donald Trump.
news.summary: Police patrols have been stepped up, and control over the transportation and storage of dangerous and explosive substances has been tightened

news.title: Mary Peltola Closes in on 50% Threshold in Alaska Senate Race
news.text: Alaska counts its ballots the way it does most things: slowly, across enormous distances, one envelope at a time. In the race for the state's U.S. Senate seat, Democrat Mary Peltola is now just 157 votes short of an outright majority. The Division of Elections' unofficial summary report, released Saturday afternoon, shows Democrat Mary Peltola with 140,637 first-choice votes, or 49.94 percent, to Republican Senator Dan Sullivan's 129,424, or 45.96 percent. Republican Gerald L. Heikes drew 6,002 votes. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired Petersburg teacher who shares the senator's name, drew 4,652, and write-ins accounted for 872. As of 8:29 a.m. Eastern on Sunday, The Associated Press estimated that 97 percent of the vote had been counted and had not called the race. The Division's first-choice count includes the 872 unresolved write-ins, which its published rules treat as a single group in the first round. That number matters because of how Alaska settles close contests. A candidate who wins more than half of first-choice votes is elected outright. If no one does, the Division of Elections begins a ranked-choice tabulation on November 18, eliminating the last-place candidate and moving those ballots to voters' next choices. A candidate who passes 50 percent in any round wins, though the Division continues counting until two candidates remain. The Arithmetic of a Majority The 157-vote gap will not hold still. Each newly counted ballot raises the bar for a majority, so Peltola cannot simply collect a handful of votes; she has to win a share of everything that remains. AP does not publish a count of outstanding ballots. Its 97 percent is a rounded estimate of the expected vote. Assuming AP rounds to the nearest point, treating that figure as anything from 96.5 to just under 97.5 percent and applying it to the Division’s total, Newsweek’s analysis estimates that several thousand Senate votes remain. To clear 50 percent on first choices alone, Peltola would need roughly 52 percent of what is left. The estimate rests on assumptions: that AP's figure applies to the Senate contest, and that every remaining ballot carries a valid Senate vote, though some voters skip races. The pool is not yet sealed, either. Ballots mailed from overseas can still arrive through November 18. Sullivan's Two Roads For the senator, the first-choice count offers little room. He trails by 11,213 votes. Under AP's estimate, Newsweek's analysis found that deficit is larger than the number of Senate votes that appear to remain. Even if every outstanding vote broke his way, Peltola would still hold more first choices, so long as the estimates hold. His other road runs through ranked choice, and it opens only if Peltola finishes below a majority. Then the race turns on something the public count does not show: how voters ordered the candidates behind their first pick. Newsweek independently ran the Division's ballot-level cast vote record, a record of how each scanned ballot ranked the candidates, which covers 282,698 ballots, through RCTab 2.0.1, open-source software built to tabulate ranked-choice elections, with settings matching the Division’s published rules for write-ins, overvotes and skipped rankings. Of those ballots, 1,059 ranked no one in the Senate race. Another 598 were inactive from the first round: 428 were overvotes, with more than one candidate marked at the same ranking, and 170 were set aside under the state's rules on skipped rankings. Alaska's tabulation removes one candidate per round. Each ballot of the eliminated candidate moves to that voter's next-ranked candidate still in the race; a ballot with no such ranking goes inactive and stops counting. In the tabulation, write-ins fall first. Of those 870 ballots, 165 move to Peltola, 117 to Sullivan, 71 to Sullivan Jr., and 125 to Heikes, while 392 go inactive. Sullivan Jr., who starts the record with 4,687 first choices, goes next, and his 4,758 ballots, including 71 picked up from write-ins, lean toward Peltola: 1,395 move to her, 753 to the senator and 861 to Heikes, while 1,749 go inactive. Heikes, who starts the record with 6,046 first choices, is eliminated last. His 7,032 ballots, including 125 from write-ins and 861 from Sullivan Jr., break the other way: 2,893 to Sullivan and 1,351 to Peltola, with 2,788 going inactive. These counts come from the November 14 cast vote record, not from the Division's first-choice totals cited above. The two don’t match exactly, and some candidates’ totals run lower in the cast vote record while others run slightly higher. One reason is documented: the record leaves out ballots counted only by hand. Differences in timing and in how first choices are tallied may also contribute; how much each accounts for has not been determined. With two candidates left, 276,112 ballots were still active; 5,527 had gone inactive along the way, including the 598 inactive from the first round, while the 1,059 blank ballots never entered the count. Newsweek's RCTab analysis of the scanned ballot records shows Peltola with 143,127 votes, or 51.83 percent, to Sullivan's 132,985, or 48.16 percent, a lead of 10,142 votes. That is Newsweek's independent model of the scanned ballots, not the state's official result. The Division says its cast vote record contains scanned ballots and leaves out those counted only by hand. The file also does not include ballots still to be tallied. The state's official tabulation will be conducted separately by the Division, using its own records and procedures as additional eligible ballots—including hand-counted ballots and mail ballots received by the deadline—are included. The 10,142-vote margin reflects only the ballots included in Newsweek's analysis; how the remaining and hand-counted ballots would affect the final comparison is not yet known. If no candidate finishes the count with a majority of first-choice votes, the official tabulation, run on the state's software, begins November 18. Earlier projections pointed in opposite directions. A memo from Sullivan's campaign, circulated soon after Election Day, projected him narrowly winning a ranked-choice count of the ballots then in hand, 105,037 to 104,709. A preliminary FairVote analysis released Thursday had Peltola winning the final round 50.1 percent to 49.9 percent. Competing Certainties Peltola's camp considers the matter closed. Her campaign has said Sullivan has "no mathematical path" to victory, and in a post on X it called her win "all but guaranteed." The figures support a narrower claim. On first choices, under AP's estimate, Sullivan trails by more than appears to remain. In Newsweek's ranked-choice tabulation, Peltola leads, but the picture is incomplete. Sullivan's campaign has not conceded. In a statement Wednesday, spokesperson Nate Adams said the campaign would "look forward to a complete and accurate count." The Other Sullivan The rankings also speak to the question that has shadowed this race for months. The New York Times reported, according to AP's race summary, that Peltola's campaign was involved in efforts to recruit Sullivan Jr., allegedly to siphon votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign has said it had no involvement with either Sullivan campaign, and Sullivan Jr. has said he ran on his own. The Justice Department sued to block certification if the senator lost but would have won had every vote for Sullivan Jr. gone to him instead, pending an investigation into whether those voters meant to choose the senator. The department’s amended complaint also sought to prevent certification while that investigation took place. A federal judge dismissed the suit November 1 for lack of standing. She also wrote that segregating ballots ranking Sullivan Jr. so voters could be investigated would violate Alaskans’ right to a secret ballot. The department has appealed. President Donald Trump also weighed in on the unusual race, posting on Truth Social on November 5 that Sullivan Jr. was "Fake Dan Sullivan." About a week after Election Day, Trump posted again, writing "Dan Sullivan PLUS Dan Sullivan" alongside a reference to the Alaska race. Wednesday Democrats have already won control of Congress. Alaska will help set the size of their Senate majority, and a Peltola victory would give the party its first Alaska Senate seat since Democrat Mark Begich lost to Sullivan in 2014. On Wednesday, the last ballots mailed from overseas are due. If no candidate has a first-round majority, the Division begins its ranked-choice tabulation, and certification is targeted for November 25. For months, this race was argued over names: which Dan, whose recruit, whose confusion. If no candidate wins outright, voters' rankings will determine which candidate wins a majority of the active ballots.
news.summary: Peltola nears 50% in Alaska’s Senate count. A Newsweek analysis breaks down what she—and Dan Sullivan—would need next.
news.author: Lars Hanson

news.title: Trump Heads to Asia for Historic Meeting With Xi and Putin: What's at Stake
news.text: President Donald Trump heads to Asia on Monday for a trip that will culminate in an unprecedented meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, bringing together the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers. The three leaders are scheduled to meet Thursday, November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The White House and Kremlin have confirmed plans for the gathering, with nuclear weapons and the war involving Iran expected to be among the subjects discussed. The meeting comes less than three weeks after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections, leaving Trump facing a changed political landscape at home as he turns his attention to diplomacy abroad. But the trilateral gathering also has conspicuous limits. U.S. officials have said Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be discussed, and Trump does not plan to raise the controversy surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials have reportedly assessed to be an asset of Chinese intelligence. The trip also puts Trump alongside senior administration officials embroiled in a public dispute over the enforcement of restrictions designed to keep advanced American computer chips out of China. Nuclear Arms and Iran on the Agenda The White House has said Trump intends to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals with Xi and Putin. A senior U.S. official characterized the gathering as the beginning of what the administration hopes will be a productive conversation, rather than a meeting expected to produce an immediate agreement. The talks come after the expiration of the New START treaty in February, ending the last remaining agreement limiting the nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. Trump rejected a Russian proposal to extend the treaty for another year, instead calling for a new agreement that would include China. The three countries have sharply different nuclear stockpiles. The United States and Russia each have more than 5,000 nuclear warheads in their total inventories, while China's arsenal is estimated at more than 600, according to U.S. assessments cited by The Associated Press. Beijing has shown little interest in joining an arms-control agreement with Washington and Moscow. Iran is also expected to feature in the discussions. The United States is directly involved in the conflict, while Russia and China maintain close relations with Tehran. A senior U.S. official said Trump intends to raise the war with both leaders, although the administration does not expect a breakthrough. The meeting offers Trump an opportunity to present himself as a leader capable of bringing the world's major nuclear powers together. But analysts have cautioned that the gathering may be more significant for its symbolism than for any immediate diplomatic results. What's Not Expected to Be Discussed Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be on the trilateral agenda, according to U.S. officials. Washington has pursued a separate diplomatic track involving Kyiv and Moscow, and the administration has said China is not part of those negotiations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not been invited to the gathering. The decision to leave Ukraine out could nevertheless draw attention. Zelenskyy has expressed concern about the prospect of the United States, Russia and China discussing issues affecting Ukraine without Kyiv's participation. Trump also does not plan to raise the controversy surrounding Alice Huang with Xi, U.S. officials have said. Newsweek previously reported that U.S. intelligence officials assessed Huang to be an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. The allegations have not been independently established publicly. The controversy has drawn attention because of Huang's reported relationship with Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Nvidia has said it has no reason to believe company secrets were compromised. Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said it takes compliance seriously. The company told Reuters that Alice Huang left in August 2025 and no longer has a role there. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had not reached a conclusion about whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, while the FBI was investigating the reports. U.S. officials have also said they do not expect the administration's export-control policies to be a subject of negotiations with China during the trip. Lutnick, Bessent and the Chip Dispute That position comes as the administration faces questions about how aggressively it should restrict the flow of advanced American chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly criticized the Commerce Department's handling of Megaspeed, saying Treasury, Defense, State, and the U.S. Trade Representative had supported placing the company on the Commerce Department's Entity List for months. The designation would restrict its access to American technology. "Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC. He said he was frustrated by what he described as the leakage of advanced U.S. chips to China. Axios reported that Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over the delay in adding Megaspeed to the list. The Commerce Department denied that the two Cabinet officials had the conversation. Bessent did not publicly confirm the reported confrontation. Elon Musk has also figured in the administration's internal discussions. Axios reported that Trump consulted Musk during a meeting about restricting suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China, with Musk supporting tighter controls. Musk is expected to accompany Trump for portions of the Asia trip but will not participate in the trilateral meeting, U.S. officials have said. Trump will also meet separately with Xi, with the two leaders expected to discuss implementation of their trade agreement. U.S. officials have said Trump is unhappy with the pace and volume of China's rare-earth shipments and intends to raise the issue. The trip comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, giving them greater oversight authority over the administration's foreign policy and trade decisions. The midterm losses have also raised questions about Trump's political standing as he seeks to demonstrate influence abroad. The gathering in Shenzhen will give Trump a rare opportunity to sit down with Xi and Putin at the same time. Whether it produces progress on nuclear arms, Iran, or other issues remains uncertain, while the administration's disputes over China policy are likely to follow the president overseas. news.summary: Trump heads to Asia for a historic meeting with Xi and Putin, with nuclear arms and Iran in focus, and Ukraine left out.
news.author: Steven Frank

news.title: ‘60 Minutes’ Exposes Shock Scale of Trump’s War Humiliation
news.text:
60 Minutes has pulled back the curtain on the true scale of devastation President Donald Trump’s war with Iran has wrought.

CBS News’ Norah O’Donnell revealed in Sunday’s episode that Iran has struck at least 31 U.S. military and diplomatic sites across the Middle East since Trump began the war in February, citing video and the network’s analysis of satellite imagery.

The Pentagon, under the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has only selectively recognized attacks on U.S. bases during the nearly nine-month conflict, which has made it difficult for Americans to gauge a clear assessment of the damage caused by Iran.

“Our analysis of satellite imagery and new video shows the scale of destruction the Pentagon has never fully disclosed,” O’Donnell said. “Since the start of the war, Iran has hit at least 31 U.S. military and diplomatic sites across eight countries, damaging hundreds of buildings and structures–from Saudi Arabia, to Kuwait, to Bahrain, where the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet was destroyed.”

O’Donnell added that despite Trump’s assertion that the war was won on April 1, strikes have continued in both directions for months.

On Sunday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps fired six drones toward a U.S. air defense radar facility in Bahrain. But the country’s military said the drones were shot down “before they could achieve their objectives,” according to the BBC.

Since the start of the war, 23 U.S. service members have been killed, and more than 800 have been wounded, according to the Pentagon’s official database.

The Defense Department has publicly acknowledged only mass casualty events during the conflict, such as the Iranian strike on a U.S. base in Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, on March 1, which killed six American service members.

The day after the missile strike, which was the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the conflict so far, Hegseth described it to reporters as a “squirter” that snuck through air defenses to hit what he called a “fortified” tactical operations center.

But Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who survived the Iranian strike, said the fortifications at the military operations center were subpar.

“I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself—all the way down to my level,” Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. “We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn.”

The veteran has filed a complaint with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, alleging that military leadership is responsible for the deaths of his six fellow troops.

In the complaint, obtained by CBS News, Ramsbottom said top military brass ignored concerns about thin fortifications and described the Port Shuaiba command post as having “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance.”

Joey Amor, the widowed husband of Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, who died in the Port Shuaiba attack, went a step further in his critique of Pentagon leadership.

“If I’m being frank, it’s—it’s on them. They killed my wife,” Amor told 60 Minutes. They killed these soldiers. And it’s not political. There are individuals in that command that made choices."

The Daily Beast has reached out to the Pentagon and the White House for comment.

Trump, 80, acknowledged that his unpopular war with Iran influenced his party’s historic rout in the midterm elections, but has maintained that the conflict was necessary.

The president has repeatedly stated that he would make the same decision to attack Iran again if it meant it would prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Trump told reporters last week that the conflict is “effectively over” and that the U.S. is simply maintaining the “status quo” at the request of its allies in the Persian Gulf.

He also falsely claimed during a pair of interviews on Thursday that no U.S. troops had been killed during the past five months, despite at least four American service members having died in July alone.

On Sunday night, the president posted a video on Truth Social of American troops praying in unison with the caption, “May God protect our troops say AMEN.”

CBS News’ Norah O’Donnell revealed in Sunday’s episode that Iran has struck at least 31 U.S. military and diplomatic sites across the Middle East since Trump began the war in February, citing video and the network’s analysis of satellite imagery.

The Pentagon, under the leadership of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, has only selectively recognized attacks on U.S. bases during the nearly nine-month conflict, which has made it difficult for Americans to gauge a clear assessment of the damage caused by Iran.

news.title: 2027: Ex-INEC REC, Mike Igini, Writes Trump, Seeks US Sanctions Against Election Riggers
news.text:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

A former Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), Mike Igini, has written to President Donald Trump, urging his administration to impose targeted sanctions, including visa restrictions and asset freezes, on Nigerian electoral officials, judges and security personnel found culpable of electoral fraud ahead of the 2027 general election.

Igini, in the letter dated November 13, 2026, also urged the US government to deploy high-level diplomatic engagement and independent election monitoring to Nigeria, arguing that credible elections and accountable leadership could help address some of the underlying causes of illegal migration from the country.

The letter was titled: ‘No Mandate from Fraud Election 2027: A Policy Using Electoral Integrity to Reduce Illegal Immigration from Nigeria’.

The former INEC commissioner proposed that the Trump administration should adopt and announce the ‘No Mandate Fraud’ doctrine ahead of the presidential election, combining preventive diplomacy, independent monitoring and targeted accountability for confirmed electoral violations.

On the proposed sanctions, Igini called on the US, in consultation with its European partners, to send a clear warning to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and all personnel involved in conducting the 2027 elections that deliberate manipulation of results and other serious electoral offences would attract individual consequences.

He identified the INEC chairman, national commissioners, resident electoral commissioners and ad hoc personnel drawn from federal agencies and universities as key officials whose conduct would be critical to the integrity of the exercise.

Igini proposed that those found, on the basis of credible evidence, to have manipulated results, falsified electoral records or committed other serious electoral offences should face visa restrictions and, where legally justified, targeted financial sanctions and asset freezes.

The ex-INEC commissioner argued that such measures, subject to applicable legal requirements, would make electoral malpractice personally costly for those entrusted with protecting the integrity of the ballot.

“Officials who engaged in the deliberate manipulation of results, falsification of electoral records or other serious electoral offences established by credible evidence, and who meet the applicable legal criteria for sanctions, should face appropriate individual and immediate family members consequences, including visa restrictions and, where legally justified, targeted financial sanctions and asset freezes,” he suggested.

Making a case for linking American immigration policy to electoral integrity in Nigeria, the renowned lawyer argued that the country’s persistent leadership failures, electoral malpractice, corruption and insecurity had contributed to the conditions driving Nigerians abroad.

“Mr President, Nigerians are not leaving Nigeria because they do not love their country. They are leaving because of decades of persistent electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and weak public accountability that have undermined Nigerians’ confidence in government and contributed to the conditions that compel many to seek opportunities abroad, including in the United States,” he wrote.

He argued that Nigeria, despite its enormous human and natural resources, has failed to translate its potential into prosperity because of the manner in which political leadership is recruited.

“Nigeria has the population, oil, gas, and talent to be one of the richest nations on earth. But undermined by leadership recruitment process that has rendered the country a plundered wilderness, littered with the debris of missed opportunities, this has forced thousands of professionals, students and families to seek refuge in the United States,” he stated.

According to him, migration has multiple causes, but credible elections remain fundamental to establishing legitimate leadership, strengthening public institutions and creating the conditions for sustainable prosperity.

“The challenge is how to ensure that public office derives authority and legitimacy from the freely expressed will of the electorate and that those entrusted with power govern in the public interest,” he said, adding that border enforcement alone cannot solve the problem.

Igini also extended his proposed accountability measures to the judiciary, warning that judicial independence should not be used to shield deliberate corruption or the subversion of electoral justice.

“Judicial independence is indispensable to democracy, but it must not become a shield for deliberate corruption or subversion of electoral justice,” he stated.

He urged the Trump administration to consider appropriate measures against individual judicial officers whose deliberate corruption or other sanctionable misconduct was established by credible evidence and met the applicable legal criteria for designation.

On the conduct of security agencies, Igini said the Nigeria Police Force (NPF), Department of State Services (DSS), armed forces, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) and other security institutions have a responsibility to protect citizens and uphold the law impartially rather than serve the interests of politicians.

He noted that the growing violence and thuggery accompanying political campaigns made impartial security enforcement particularly important ahead of the elections.

The former commissioner urged the US government to hold senior officers and commanders accountable where credible evidence established that they authorised or facilitated voter intimidation, electoral violence, unlawful suppression of opposition or manipulation of election outcomes.

He said such officers should face appropriate individual consequences, including visa restrictions and other sanctions.

Beyond sanctions, Igini proposed high-level diplomatic intervention by the United States ahead of the elections, recommending that Trump dispatch a senior delegation to engage President Bola Tinubu, presidential and governorship candidates, INEC, political parties and other relevant institutions.

He said the delegation should make clear that credible elections, peaceful political competition and respect for constitutional rights were core American national interests, with direct implications for bilateral engagement, migration and stability.

He also urged Washington to support credible domestic and international election observers to monitor the process before, during and after the polls, with particular attention to voter intimidation, the impartial conduct of security personnel, publication of polling-unit results, transparent collation and the resolution of electoral disputes.

Igini argued that the combination of diplomatic pressure, independent monitoring and evidence-based sanctions could deter electoral violations and strengthen public confidence in Nigeria’s democratic process.

Explaining the benefits of his proposal to the US, he identified reduced migration pressure, protection of American resources, improved security cooperation and stronger economic relations as key advantages.

On migration, he argued that credible elections would make it possible for Nigerians to elect leaders capable of addressing the country’s economic and institutional problems, reducing the incentive for citizens to seek opportunities abroad.

“Credible elections produce good leaders. Good leaders fix the economy. When Nigeria works, Nigerians will stay home and build their country. Many in the US diaspora will return,” he wrote.

He also maintained that the US should stop legitimising and funding governments that lacked the consent of their people, arguing that a stable, democratic and accountable Nigeria would be a stronger partner in tackling terrorism, organised crime, regional insecurity and adversarial influence in Africa.

On economic cooperation, Igini said credible leadership would also advance shared American and Nigerian interests, particularly in the energy sector, where US companies could provide technology and expertise to governments committed to improving electricity supply and diversifying energy sources.

In his appeal for urgent action, he urged Trump to communicate the proposed policy before the elections rather than wait for electoral disputes and a possible crisis.

“Mr President, strength and clarity work. The time to act is before the election, not after a crisis has occurred. To save American money and border resources, a clear US message now is urgent; that America will not do business as usual with any government produced through electoral fraud,” he stated.
news.summary: Urges visa restrictions, asset freezes against culpable INEC officials, judges, security personnel  Says credible elections could stem illegal migration from Nigeria Proposes US diplomatic intervention, independent monitoring of polls  Emmanuel

news.title: Trump Criticizes California Gov. Gavin Newsom for Sparing Death Row Prisoners
news.text:
Donald Trump has launched a scathing attack on Gavin Newsom after the California governor moved to spare 548 death-row inmates from execution, arguing that the crimes committed by some of the convicted killers make Hannibal Lecter seem “like a nice guy.”

In a furious criticism of the Democratic governor, Trump mocked Newsom as “Gavin Newscum” and challenged the decision to grant clemency to prisoners convicted of horrific offenses, including the abduction and murder of a 12-year-old girl, torture killings and a mass shooting that claimed seven lives.

“Some of the people that Gavin Newscum freed from the Death Penalty, after many years of going through the California ‘Justice’ System, make Hannibal Lecter, of Silence of the Lambs, look like a nice guy!” the President wrote on Truth Social.

Trump’s broadside came as criticism intensified over Newsom’s decision to commute the death sentences of every inmate currently on California’s death row, a move that would effectively eliminate the state’s condemned population.

The prisoners affected include some of California’s most notorious murderers. One is Richard Allen Davis, who kidnapped and killed 12-year-old Polly Klaas during a sleepover at her family’s Petaluma home in October 1993.

Davis entered the house armed with a knife, restrained Polly’s two friends and took the schoolgirl from her bedroom. Her disappearance triggered a massive nationwide search. About two months later, Davis directed investigators to a shallow grave where Polly’s strangled body had been buried.

The case became one of the most infamous child murders in U.S. history and helped build public support for California’s strict Three Strikes law. Following a lengthy and contentious trial, Davis was sentenced to death in 1996.

The list also includes Charles Ng, who was convicted of taking part in the murders of 11 people alongside Leonard Lake during a brutal crime spree in the 1980s.

The two men used a remote property in Calaveras County as the base for their crimes, abducting victims and subjecting them to torture before killing them.

Their victims included men, women and children. Evidence recovered at the property revealed the disturbing extent of the operation. Ng was ultimately convicted of 11 murders and sentenced to death in 1999.

Randy Kraft, known as the “Scorecard Killer,” is another inmate whose sentence would be commuted. He was convicted of killing 16 young men, while investigators connected him to many more suspected murders.

Michael Gargiulo, dubbed the “Hollywood Ripper,” is also covered by the proposal. He was convicted of murdering two women and trying to kill another in attacks that spread fear across Southern California.

Chester Turner, referred to as the “Southside Slayer,” is likewise on the list. Turner was convicted of 14 murders, many involving women whose remains were found in and around Los Angeles.

Newsom’s plan would not release the men from prison. Their death sentences would instead be changed to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

The convictions would not be overturned, and the inmates would remain behind bars. A commutation is neither a pardon nor an acquittal; it reduces or changes a sentence without altering the underlying guilty verdict.

The governor’s announcement has nevertheless drawn intense opposition. Prosecutors have accused Newsom of using poor judgment and of treating cases with vastly different circumstances as if they were all the same.

Newsom also faces a major legal hurdle. Of the 548 inmates, 382 have multiple felony convictions and need a recommendation from the California Supreme Court before their death sentences can be reduced. Prosecutors are supporting a legal challenge to the governor’s blanket policy.

Newsom has defended the decision as a principled rejection of capital punishment, saying California should not execute prisoners on behalf of the state.

“I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” he said.

He placed a moratorium on executions in March 2019, shortly after becoming governor. California’s last execution took place in January 2006.

For the families of victims, however, the decision has revived pain surrounding cases that have remained emotionally raw for years.

Marc Klaas, whose daughter Polly was killed by Davis, said Newsom’s announcement felt like “a shiv in my back.”

Victims’ rights groups and prosecutors have echoed Klaas’s anger, arguing that the sweeping commutations overlook the suffering of families who spent years or even decades navigating the courts before death sentences were imposed.

Trump’s remarks represent another highly public clash with Newsom, whom he has repeatedly attacked over California’s progressive policies.

Newsom, widely viewed as a potential future Democratic presidential candidate, has frequently been targeted by Trump, who portrays California’s liberal leadership as a symbol of what he considers the Democratic Party’s failures.

While Newsom says he is rejecting government-sanctioned executions, Trump has made clear that he views the governor’s policy as unjustifiable leniency toward prisoners convicted of exceptionally brutal crimes.

news.title: Indian rupee caught between external pressures and foreign inflows
news.text:
MUMBAI: The Indian rupee is expected to open largely flat on Monday, caught between higher US bond yields, dollar ​strength and volatile oil prices, while a revival in foreign ‌portfolio inflows cushions the pressure.

The Indian rupee is expected to open in the 94.22 to 94.28 range, per traders, having settled at 94.24 to the dollar ​on Friday.

The currency, which had been on a winning ​run, came under pressure late last week, largely weighed down ⁠by a surge in US Treasury yields that lifted the ​dollar index to its highest level in a year and a ​half.

The rupee scaled a high of 93.60 before losing momentum and slipping back past the 94 mark.

“It’s increasingly difficult to call the next move. You cannot ​ignore the kind of foreign inflows we have seen. At the ​same time, these levels are good for importers to step up hedging,” a currency ‌trader ⁠at a private-sector bank said.

Although the rise in US yields is a concern, the trader said that foreign inflows make it difficult to turn outright bearish on the rupee.

Overseas investors have bought nearly $9 ​billion worth of ​Indian equities so ⁠far this month, marking a major turnaround from outflows of around $3.5 billion each in September and ​October.

Meanwhile, lingering uncertainty over a possible US-Iran deal has ​driven ⁠a recovery in oil prices from recent lows, adding to the rupee’s external headwinds.

Oil prices face competing pressures, with reports that US President ⁠Donald Trump ​may hold off on further attacks against ​Iran offering some relief, while Tehran’s claim that it struck a US base in ​Bahrain keeps escalation risks alive.

news.title: PM Modi's Manila Visit: What's On Agenda? ASEAN Summit, Maritime, Economics Ties And More
news.text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will on Monday visit Manila to participate in the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and 21st East Asia Summit, as India looks to strengthen its strategic and economic engagement with Southeast Asia.Modi is visiting Manila at the invitation of Philippine's President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., with the Philippines hosting the regional gatherings as ASEAN Chair fir 2026.The visit comes at a significant time, with 2026 being observed as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation. India and ASEAN will also mark 35 years of Dialogue Relations and five years of their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2027, the Prime Minister's Office stated.ALSO READ: Prince William, Kate Middleton To Meet PM Modi During India VisitPrime Minister's Departure Statement Ahead Of Visit"Our relationship with ASEAN countries is at the heart of India's Act East Policy and occupies a central place in our MAHASAGAR vision. Our ties, rooted in centuries of civilizational exchanges, have grown into a dynamic partnership spanning trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations.At the ASEAN-India Summit, I look forward to working with fellow leaders to build on the progress of our Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and give further momentum to our shared aspirations for growth, connectivity and prosperity.The East Asia Summit provides an important platform for dialogue on regional and global challenges. I look forward to exchanging views with participating leaders on strengthening peace, stability and cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.I also look forward to interacting with the vibrant Indian community in the Philippines, whose contributions strengthen the bonds of friendship between our two countries.I am confident that the visit will impart new energy to India's partnership with ASEAN and reinforce our collective commitment to a peaceful, prosperous and resilient Indo-Pacific."What's on Agenda?The 23rd ASEAN-India Summit will review progress in the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and assess the implementation of the ASEAN-India Plan of Action 2026–2030, according to the PMO.The summit will also provide an opportunity for leaders to discuss the future direction of cooperation between India and the Southeast Asian bloc.Addressing a media briefing ahead of the visit, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) Secretary (East) Rudrendra Tandon described India's engagement with ASEAN as an important building block of the country's Act East Policy.Tandon stated that India's relationship with ASEAN, both collectively and through individual member states, was important for strengthening regional resilience amid rapid geopolitical changes.The theme of this year's ASEAN Summit and related processes is 'Navigating the Future', with discussions expected to focus on improving regional cooperation and resilience, according to Tandon.Maritime CooperationMaritime cooperation is expected to be among the major priorities during Modi's engagements in Manila because India and ASEAN have designated 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation. The initiative places greater emphasis on maritime safety, security and economic cooperation. According to the MEA, India considers maritime engagement an important component of its relationship with ASEAN. Ahead of the Prime Minister's visit, MEA Secretary Rudrendra Tandon highlighted maritime domain awareness, coordinated patrolling and cooperation against piracy and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing as important areas of engagement with ASEAN countries. Tandon also said that India could contribute through maritime training and capacity-building assistance to strengthen the capabilities of regional partners.India-ASEAN Economic TiesEconomic cooperation is said to be an important component of the Prime Minister's visit. MEA Secretary Rudrendra Tandon said India's trade with the ASEAN region stood at approximately $122 billion, underlining the importance of the bloc as a major economic partner.India is also seeking to complete the review of the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), which came into force in 2010.According to Tandon, New Delhi wants the review process to be completed as soon as possible, although negotiations remain complex because they require consensus among ASEAN's member countries.The review is significant for India because it seeks to improve market access for Indian exporters and address concerns surrounding trade imbalances.Tandon also said that India was pursuing discussions with individual ASEAN countries on trade facilitation and trade agreements to create additional opportunities for Indian businesses.India-ASEAN Defence TiesDefence cooperation is another important part of the India-Philippines relationship. One of the most significant developments in bilateral defence ties was the $375 million agreement signed in January 2022 for the supply of India's BrahMos shore-based anti-ship missile systems to the Philippines.The agreement marked an important milestone in India's defence exports and strengthened defence cooperation between the two countries. It also demonstrated India's growing role as a defence equipment supplier in Southeast Asia. The Philippines' geographical position and maritime interests also make defence and security cooperation relevant to India's broader Indo-Pacific engagement.MEA Secretary Tandon highlighted India's existing defence cooperation with several ASEAN member states, including the Philippines, while discussing the region's strategic importance.Modi-Donald Trump MeetA possible meeting between Modi and US President Donald Trump could happen. However, there is no official confirmation. The meeting, if held, would provide an opportunity for the two leaders to discuss bilateral relations and wider geopolitical developments. East Asia Summit processAfter the India-ASEAN Summit, the Prime Minister will then participate in the 21st East Asia Summit process, said Rudrendra Tandon.The East Asia Summit process is also a very unique ASEAN-led grouping of eight leaders, where it's a leaders-led forum, said Tondon, adding, "The leaders of ASEAN and these eight countries basically discuss, in an informal setting, global security issues and issues of common concern. This year's East Asia Summit process is led by the ASEAN Chair, which is the Philippines. That's why it's happening in Manila. This, too, is a remarkable example of how successful ASEAN collective diplomacy has become."Why Is Prime Minister's Visit Significant?Modi's Philippines visit brings together India's economic, diplomatic and maritime priorities in Southeast Asia. The ASEAN-India Summit will provide an opportunity to review the existing strategic partnership, while the East Asia Summit will allow India to engage with regional and global powers on wider geopolitical concerns.With maritime cooperation being a designated priority for 2026, discussions on maritime security, regional stability and freedom of navigation are expected to remain important.The visit also offers India and the Philippines an opportunity to build on their existing defence relationship and explore further cooperation in technology, infrastructure, digital payments and investment.ALSO READ: Why Has Netanyahu Sent Israel's Spy Chief To Washington Amid Iran War Tensions?
news.summary: As India looks to deepen its engagement with the Indo-Pacific, the Manila meetings are an important part of its continuing diplomatic outreach to Southeast Asia.

news.title: Asian shares fall before Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO test tech rally
news.text:
SYDNEY: Asian shares fell on Monday after a whiplash week capped by the shock exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, with the chipmaker’s earnings and Anthropic’s IPO this week set to ​test whether the AI-fuelled bull market still has further to run.

Also later in the week, US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi ‌Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen to discuss nuclear arms reduction and the US-Israeli war with Iran.

The minutes of the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting are due on Wednesday, while a parade of Fed speakers will also be on the bill this week. Markets will be alert for any hint of policymakers being receptive to the ​idea of an outsized 50-basis-point interest rate hike next month.

In Asia on Monday, Japan’s Nikkei fell 0.6%, while South Korea slipped 0.2%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific ​shares outside Japan eased 0.1%.

S&P 500 futures edged up 0.3%, while Nasdaq futures bounced 0.5%.

Nvidia, the poster child of a four-year US ⁠bull market, has seen its market value tumble from about $5.8 trillion in early October to $3.9 trillion as of Friday, LSEG data showed, as investors rushed for the exit after ​Huang’s departure.

Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of $109 billion in Nvidia’s fiscal third quarter when its earnings are due on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with all eyes on ​whether the chipmaker will stick to its bullish outlook for next year under new management.

“Options markets imply an earnings-day move of approximately +/-7%, yet I question whether the quarterly numbers will carry their usual significance,” said Chris Weston, head of research at foreign exchange brokerage Pepperstone.

“Nvidia may well deliver another exceptional beat and raise at tomorrow’s earnings, but investors are increasingly trying to value a business in FY2028 ​and FY2029 potentially without the individual who architected its competitive advantage.”

The Financial Times reported Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning as CEO. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said ​Nvidia needs to “go outside the company” for a new CEO.

Just two days after Nvidia’s earnings, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is scheduled to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on ‌the AI ⁠trade. The firm’s IPO has drawn more institutional interest than SpaceX, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

US Dollar lifts with yields

Data on Friday showed US producer prices rose in October a touch less than markets had expected, though there were signs that inflation pressure was broadening. Together with a hotter-than-forecast consumer price index report, Friday’s figures led analysts to estimate a 0.3% rise in core personal consumption expenditure for October, which would be the third successive monthly increase at that pace.

The PCE index is the Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation when ​considering whether to change its policy interest ​rate.

Fed funds futures imply a quarter-point rate ⁠hike next month is essentially locked in, while odds for a 50-basis-point move lengthened to 6% from 12% a day earlier. A total tightening of 90 basis points is priced in by late next year.

In San Francisco on Monday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is set to ​tell a public forum that artificial intelligence will reshape the US economy, but how the region’s new tech boom evolves, and ​on what timetable, is a wild ⁠card for central bankers.

Ten-year yields were flat at 5.1433%, having jumped 29 bps to be back above the psychologically important 5% ⁠level.

The US dollar ​lifted with yield support, rising 1.1% last week against major peers to its highest since April last ​year. The dollar index was steady at 103.42 on Monday.

In commodities, oil prices were mostly steady after two weeks of decline. Brent futures fell 0.2% to $95.69 a barrel, having dropped 2.5% last week, while US crude futures ​edged 0.1% higher to $88.68, after falling by a similar amount last week.

Non-interest-bearing gold bounced 0.3% to $3,891 an ounce , having fallen 4.6% last week.

In recent days, the Treasury chief has also pointed a finger at the Commerce Department for failing to do enough to enforce US export curbs."This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," Bessent said in an interview on Fox News's Sunday Morning Futures. "They need a dramatic shakeup."READ | 'Chinese Spy' Alice Huang Left Company In 2025: Megaspeed Amid Nvidia RowYet hours after Bessent's interview aired, the Financial Times reported that Huang has been discussing the idea of returning to the company he co-founded more than three decades ago, with some Silicon Valley supporters putting together a "war room" to gather support. Nvidia and a Huang spokesperson declined to comment.A perpetual futures contract on the Hyperliquid blockchain referencing Nvidia's share price rose as much as 4.5 percent after the FT report.Revelations that Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the US suspects of being a Chinese spy, have forced a reckoning for the company that's played a critical role in driving the AI boom. The former Nvidia chief evangelized AI adoption and enlisted President Donald Trump as an ally to clear the path of regulations that could stymie growth of the technology.In the wake of Jensen Huang's resignation, Bessent said he wants to know whether Nvidia intentionally ignored warning signs of shell companies, many of them in Singapore, funneling chips to China, signaling he wants to shift the focus from the departed CEO's personal "foibles" to the legal and national-security aspects."I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said. "And I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."The US Justice Department is spearheading an investigation into Megaspeed over suspected semiconductor smuggling and is also probing whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in efforts to smuggle products made by Super Micro Computer Inc. to China, Bloomberg News has reported. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, and Super Micro has said Megaspeed was never one of its customers.Nvidia's board has launched an internal inquiry into its former CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, though it has also said that it doesn't believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Federal law enforcement authorities have an espionage investigation underway, along with the probes of possible chip smuggling, while key committees in Congress are kicking off their own reviews.READ | 'Without Jensen Huang, Handshake Deals Will Be Lost': Musk Warns NvidiaHuang has agreed to testify before House lawmakers behind closed doors on his relationship with Alice Huang, according to Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. His panel and two others are still sorting a date with Huang, and members are eager to understand whether any sensitive information may have been exposed, Moolenaar said on CBS's Face the Nation.Nvidia's efforts to intervene in inquiries risk also drawing scrutiny from US lawmakers. The company appealed to Taiwanese officials after prosecutors on the island accused an Nvidia employee of helping to smuggle AI chips into China, Bloomberg News has reported. Nvidia raised its concerns to political officials about the manager's July arrest, Bloomberg reported.The case in Taiwan is separate from the investigation by US authorities into possible export control breaches by Megaspeed. In late summer 2025, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter called the head of a Commerce Department bureau that enforces export curbs to ask whether the agency had played a role in the detention of Alice Huang by Singapore authorities, Bloomberg News has reported.Moolenaar, along with the heads of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs panels, have also asked Teter to appear next month to answer questions about the company's adherence to export controls and news reports about what the lawmakers characterized as the company's "interference in US export controls policies and investigations."Nvidia has said in response to the Bloomberg reporting on Teter's call that it regularly consults with government officials to answer questions and provide information.The Commerce Department's handling of export controls has drawn attention from Congress but also from within the administration. Democrats, who officially take majority control of the House and Senate in January, are also eager to hear from Lutnick."It looks like he has been the barrier inside the government to stopping the flow of these Nvidia chips to China," Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence panel, said on CBS's Face the Nation. "It is the Commerce secretary's job and the president's job to stop that from happening."READ | Cousins To Rivals: How Jensen Huang's Fall Could Help AMD's Lisa Su In AI Chip RaceA spokesperson for Lutnick told NBC News last week that he had agreed to testify before Congress.Meanwhile at Nvidia, the board has begun its search for candidates to replace Huang, though the effort remains in early stages. First, the company must get through its quarterly report on Tuesday, which promises to be one of the most closely watched in recent memory.A key question will be how executives on the call address the succession issue. While Nvidia shares fell 12.7% last week, some high-profile shareholders have expressed support for Huang, including his possible return to the chipmaker he turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.In a social media post, Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited "the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang's leadership over a long period of time" and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a "slow, measured, and deliberate" approach to Nvidia's future leadership.That should include "the potential return of Jensen Huang," Altimeter's Brad Gerstner and Atreides' Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia's board posted on X. SpaceX and Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk, another Huang ally, has also voiced his support for a comeback, signing an online petition.Yet Bessent's demands for significant change at the company and the circumstances of Huang's departure make the odds of his return small. Moolenaar, whose committee focuses on China's strategic rivalry with the US, suggested the ousted CEO should have known that "every Chinese national" can be pressured to spy by the Communist Party."That was simply irresponsible and a direct threat to our national security," he said.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Rupee likely to open flat as dollar strength, US bond yields weigh on sentiment
news.text: MUMBAI The Indian rupee is expected to open largely flat on Monday, caught between higher US bond yields, dollar strength and volatile oil prices, while a revival in foreign portfolio inflows cushions the pressure. The rupee is expected to open in the 94.22 to 94.28 range, according to traders, having settled at 94.24 to the dollar on Friday. US bond yields and dollar strength weigh on rupee The currency, which had been on a winning run, came under pressure late last week, largely weighed down by a surge in US Treasury yields that lifted the dollar index to its highest level in a year and a half. The rupee scaled a high of 93.60 before losing momentum and slipping back past the 94 mark. “It’s increasingly difficult to call the next move. You cannot ignore the kind of foreign inflows we have seen. At the same time, these levels are good for importers to step up hedging,” a currency trader at a private-sector bank said. Although the rise in US yields is a concern, the trader said that foreign inflows make it difficult to turn outright bearish on the rupee. Foreign inflows provide support Overseas investors have bought nearly $9 billion worth of Indian equities so far this month, marking a major turnaround from outflows of around $3.5 billion each in September and October. Oil prices and US-Iran tensions add to uncertainty Meanwhile, lingering uncertainty over a possible US-Iran deal has driven a recovery in oil prices from recent lows, adding to the rupee’s external headwinds. Oil prices face competing pressures, with reports that US President Donald Trump may hold off on further attacks against Iran offering some relief, while Tehran’s claim that it struck a US base in Bahrain keeps escalation risks alive.
news.summary: The currency is navigating competing global pressures, with stronger foreign investor interest offering some support against rising external risks.

news.text:
PERTH: Oil ​prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus as shipments from the Middle East ‌through the Strait of Hormuz have been nearly restored to pre-war levels and the US took steps to support moving fuel cargoes between domestic ports.

Brent futures were down 47 cents, or 0.49%, to $95.37 a barrel by 0145 GMT.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 23 ​cents, or 0.26%, to $88.33.

Oil closed lower on Friday as the market weighed signs of lowering geopolitical risk ​from the US-Israeli war against Iran, now in its ninth month.

The benchmarks fell 16% ⁠and 13%, respectively, the prior week.

The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this ​year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued ​attacks on shipping.

“For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness.

That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone,“ said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.

Oil supply will average 105 ​million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said.

The ​IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit.

The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release ‌of ⁠oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness.

Prices were also pressured down by the US decision to extend a waiver of a shipping law that will continue to allow foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and ​fuels such as gasoline and ​diesel more easily between ⁠US ports.

US President Donald Trump extended for 90 days a waiver of the Jones Act, which requires US-flagged ships to carry cargo between US ports, a White House official said on ​Friday.

Waiving the rule opens up the number of tankers available to carry commodities between ​US ports.

Still, ⁠Waterer noted that while supply was loosening, shipping rates remained high, putting a floor on oil prices.

Rates remain high because of the risks the tankers face carrying crude through the Strait of Hormuz and because the number of ships tied up ⁠in shuttling ​oil through the waterway for transfer to other ships that take shipments ​to refineries has reduced the vessel supply.

On Sunday night, Iran’s navy said that an oil tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine east of ​the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.

news.title: GOP Rebel Claims New Jan. 6 Video Points to ‘Inside Job’
news.text:
Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie has suggested that the Jan. 6 pipe bomb attempt was an inside job. 

On Sunday, Massie reposted video from journalist Steve Baker, who was fired from The Blaze last year over a related story that the conservative outlet later retracted. 

The footage appears to show a Capitol police officer monitoring the Democratic National Committee headquarters around the time authorities identified an explosive device near the building. 

Baker argues that the officer’s movements and apparent failure to respond to radio calls for “all available units” suggest he knew where the device was located. The footage does not independently establish that. 

“New video reveals former Capitol Hill Police Officer behaving as if he knew about the DNC pipe bomb before it was found, and anxiously awaited its discovery,” Massie wrote on X. “More evidence suggests the J6 pipe bombs were part of an inside job or botched training exercise that’s being covered-up.”

A report Baker wrote for Blaze Media in November 2025 claimed that a former Capitol Police officer had the same distinctive walk as the pipe-bomb suspect. The outlet retracted the story the following month after the FBI arrested Brian Cole Jr. in connection with the crime and fired Baker in April.

Baker himself pleaded guilty to four misdemeanor charges related to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot. He was among those pardoned by President Donald Trump in January 2025.

Massie has previously suggested that the planting of the pipe bombs could have been an “inside job” or a “botched training exercise” as part of a larger government conspiracy to incite violence during the Jan. 6 attack. 

Massie and then-FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino clashed last year after the congressman posted a screenshot of a letter from an attorney representing an FBI whistleblower. 

The letter said the whistleblower had made a “protected disclosure” about the FBI’s investigation into the pipe bombs planted ahead of Jan. 6. Massie tagged FBI Director Kash Patel in the post, saying that federal law prohibited retaliation against whistleblowers. Bongino responded the following day, accusing Massie of implying that FBI leadership was targeting investigators. 

“America is waking up today to learn that Capitol Police turned CIA orchestrated the pipe bombs on January 6th, and the FBI has covered it up for over fours years,” Massie wrote at the time. 

Bongino called Massie’s claims a “BS bomb,” posting photos of brief phone calls between the two officials. 

Earlier this year, Massie scrutinized the federal indictment against suspect Brian J.Cole Jr., who is charged with four federal counts related to the pipe bombs. Cole has pleaded non-guilty and his trial has been set for February. 

“I believe [the] FBI arrested the wrong person in the J6 pipe bomb case,” Massie wrote in March. “Analysis indicates stark physical differences between Cole and the hoodie suspect, including the manner of walking, body shape and features, eyesight, shoe size, neck length, and mannerisms 

Representatives for Massie, the FBI, DOJ and Capitol Police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
