news.title: US Air Travel May Return To Normal Today After 3 Days Of Shutdown
news.text: US air travel was expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US aviation authorities.The ground stop issued Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks, and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.As of Sunday evening more than 55 US-related flights -- those traveling within, into or out of the United States -- scheduled for Monday were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 1,960 flights cancelled on Sunday.The Trump administration sought to reassure weary flyers as questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess. READ | Trump Administration Says Airline Disruptions May Continue For Another DayThroughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.Officials blamed Friday's colossal snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system."The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration."Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began," Trump asserted.FAA chief Bryan Bedford had said Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travelers to where they need to be."So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Duffy said on ABC News."We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that."READ | 2 Years Into Second Term, Trump Blames Biden For US Flight Disruptions'I'm The Secretary'Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure, such as, he said, radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s."So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Duffy said in an interview on CNN.The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.Duffy has appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment." But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.

news.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
news.text:
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.
news.summary: PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

news.title: 'Perfectly safe' but not 'maxed out'? Trump takes Qatar jet to Asia
news.text: US President Donald Trump is set to fly to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar, but questions remain over whether the plane has undergone the extensive security upgrades that the White House had planned for MAGA supremo, NBC News reported, citing two US officials.The aircraft's planned overhaul had drawn attention in July after a security threat from Iran forced Trump to fly back from Turkey aboard a secret military plane. The incident raised questions about the security arrangements surrounding the Qatari-gifted jet.Trump is expected to visit the Philippines to attend the Asean Summit, a key gathering of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), the regional bloc's highest decision-making forum.Trump had repeatedly said the aircraft would be taken out of service for major modifications so it could “go into any territory”. In September, he said the work would “take about 60 days”. However, the aircraft continued to be used for presidential travel, including a trip to Ireland that month and several journeys during Trump's October midterm campaign blitz.According to NBC News, the plane has undergone periodic maintenance and received some improvements, but it is unclear whether the larger security upgrades have been completed. One of the officials said a longer period of upgrades was still expected, although the work would not take the full 60 days.The changes made so far have reportedly focused largely on the aircraft's interior. One official described them as “cosmetic” enhancements, which did not include the more extensive work the White House had earlier said was planned.A senior administration official declined to discuss the specific modifications, telling NBC News: “We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once. We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.”Trump had first spoken about the planned overhaul in July, saying the aircraft already had considerable capabilities but would soon be sent for further modifications.“But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.”He did not explain what the proposed upgrades would involve. The White House has also not clarified why the initial estimate of around 30 days later increased to 60 days.Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt had said in July that the aircraft was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel. However, she confirmed that further work was planned, saying it would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”You use AI every day. news.summary: US President Donald Trump is set to travel to Asia on Monday aboard the aircraft gifted by Qatar, even as questions remain over its promised security upgrades. According to NBC News, the jet has received some maintenance and cosmetic improvements, but the larger overhaul remains unclear months after an Iran-related security scare forced Trump to fly home from Turkey on a secret military plane.

news.title: Pete Buttigieg breaks with Democrats on student loan handouts, admits party ‘overtorqued’ on issue
news.text: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg admitted Sunday that he broke ranks with the Democratic Party on student loans, saying the party "overtorqued" the issue and may have dissuaded voters. During a "Pod Save America" interview, host Dan Pfeiffer remarked that many of the Democratic candidates who won in the midterm elections disagreed with the party on at least one issue, whether it be gun control or the role of oil and gas in energy. He asked Buttigieg whether he held any beliefs that ran counter to the mainstream Democratic Party. BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP "In the 2020 campaign, I definitely staked out some positions that I still believe in that weren't always kind of popular in the party," Buttigieg said. "One thing is, I think...we really overtorqued on the student loan thing. As a party, I have a very hard time explaining to my relatives in Michigan who did not go to college why they should be paying for people who do." He added, "I believe there are ways to make sure that you come out of college debt-free. I believe college should be more affordable. I don't believe in like a magic wand to fix that for everybody who borrowed money." PETE BUTTIGIEG DISTANCES HIMSELF FROM BIDEN AMID 2028 TALK, SUGGESTS 'BUILD BACK BETTER' DOESN'T WORK Though Buttigieg told Pfeiffer that he doesn't believe in a "magic" fix for student loans, he previously served under President Joe Biden, who repeatedly attempted to cancel student loan debt, even after the Supreme Court ruled against his administration in 2023. His husband, Chasten Buttigieg, was also among those frustrated at the prospect of paying student loans after COVID-19-era loan relief was set to expire in 2022. Fox News Digital reached out to Buttigieg's organization, Win the Era, for comment. Veteran Democratic strategist Julian Epstein called the student loan forgiveness a scam and congratulated Buttigieg for having enough self-awareness to acknowledge it. JOE MANCHIN WARNS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE GAINING GROUND AS DEMOCRATS REMAIN SILENT "Buttigieg shows an all-too-rare self-awareness for a Democrat elite on this issue. The student loan giveaway, also known as loan forgiveness, is a scam," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "It's welfare for the most privileged and elite amongst us that the working class has to help fund. It's Robin Hood in reverse, and it stands against everything the Democratic Party should be standing for." Another issue Buttigieg disagreed with the Democratic Party on was the two-party system itself. news.title: ‘60 Minutes’ blows the lid off 'horrible' war damage the Pentagon kept hidden
news.text:
Some political commentators were outraged Sunday after CBS News' "60 Minutes" reported on the hidden toll of the Trump administration's war in Iran. 

President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. has lost "no soldiers" in the war in Iran, even though the Pentagon has disclosed that 23 soldiers and contractors have been killed during the conflict. The number of dead and injured soldiers is likely higher than the Pentagon is admitting to, according to a "60 Minutes" analysis of satellite imagery and videos taken in countries neighboring Iran where U.S. troops are stationed. 

"Since the start of the war, Iran has hit at least 31 military and diplomatic sites across eight countries, damaging hundreds of buildings and structures, from Saudi Arabia to Kuwait and Bahrain, where the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet was destroyed," Norah O'Donnell said during the segment. "The attacks continued for months, even after President Trump declared victory on April 1."

Widows of the dead service members told "60 Minutes" that their loved ones had expressed concerns about their ability to defend themselves from such attacks because of where they were stationed and the weapons they had. 

Some viewers were outraged by the segment, especially among critics of the administration. 

Sophia A. Nelson, a national opinion columnist, was outraged by the report. 

"This is horrible!" she posted on X.

Tim Massie, a former journalist and public relations professional, argued in a post on X that Republicans in Congress must be okay with the deaths because they have yet to rein in the president's war powers. 

"Republicans must be OK with this — death and injury to our service members; the destruction of billions, if not more than a trillion dollars in equipment and supplies; damage to the aura of invincibility the Trump Administration believes the U.S. military portrays worldwide," Massie posted. 

Bruce Crossing, a military veteran and political commentator, argued that Trump should be impeached for the deaths. 

"This isn’t victory. Hegseth should be fired. Trump should be impeached," Crossing posted on X.

news.title: Southeast Asian leaders denounce violence in Myanmar and extend ban on its leader
news.text:
MANILA: Southeast Asian leaders said Sunday that Myanmar has failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan and that its military and other armed groups continue to attack civilians, prompting them to extend a ban on Myanmar’s leader attending the bloc’s annual summits.

The stern rebuke by leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, who opened their annual summit meetings in the Philippine capital on Sunday, came after a review of the progress on the five-point peace plan by the country’s military-backed government. Myanmar is a member of the 11-nation regional bloc.

ASEAN leaders approved the plan in April 2021 to try to ease the violence that erupted after the army seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi. The army’s takeover triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.

The leaders reiterated “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the peace plan. They urged all parties and stakeholders in Myanmar, “in particular the armed forces, security forces and armed groups to de-escalate violence and stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure and enhance trust-building efforts.”

Last month, a United Nations rights investigator said the military-backed government in Myanmar was intentionally attacking civilians to terrorize them and force them into submission.

According to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners, an independent organization that keeps detailed tallies of arrests and casualties linked to the civil war, more than 8,600 people have been killed and 32,406 arrested by Myanmar’s security forces as of Friday.

The leaders said the ban on Myanmar’s leader and foreign minister attending ASEAN summit meetings would continue “until there is meaningful progress in the implementation” of the peace plan. The plan calls for, among other things, an immediate end to hostilities and the start of a dialogue mediated by the regional bloc’s special envoy.

Under the ban, Myanmar can be represented only by lower-level career diplomats, including at the ongoing ASEAN meetings in Manila. Myanmar was due to hold ASEAN’s rotating chair this year and host its multiple regional meetings, but because of the civil strife, the role passed to the Philippines.

“There’s still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people so step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we’ll monitor that,” Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, ASEAN’s current special envoy to Myanmar, said in a news conference in Manila.

The three-day ASEAN summit, which includes scheduled talks with world leaders led by US President Donald Trump, will focus on conflicts, including the civil war in Myanmar, according to drafts of post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press.

Min Aung Hlaing, who led the overthrow of Suu Kyi’s government in February 2021 as the then-army chief, was sworn in as president in April following an election held in phases in December and January. Critics dismissed the polls as a sham designed to consolidate the military’s grip on power while ostensibly restoring civilian rule.

Since then, he has visited five ASEAN member states, including Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam, in a diplomatic outreach to reengage Asian countries and the international community in his effort to win political legitimacy. Despite those visits, he has remained largely isolated internationally.

ASEAN has not discouraged those visits to its member states, but its leaders underscored that the peace plan remains “the main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar.”

Depending on “sustained and concrete progress in the implementation” of the peace plan, “ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the leaders said without elaborating.

news.title: Tough Times
news.text:
Press freedom has, for years, been under attack almost everywhere across the globe, but the situation has never been as grave as it is now. The recent findings of Reporters Without Borders (RSF) reveal the conditions for journalists in more than half of the 180 countries it surveys are “difficult” or “very serious” this year. The rising waves of war worldwide and the emergence of autocratic leaders at the helm of affairs in many countries are also increasing the pressures and dangers. A telling finding is that a new peak of 129 deaths of reporters have so far occurred in different countries within this year. The worse aspect of the oppression of journalists and the shackling of free speech, as the UNESCO remarked, is that almost “nine out of 10 killings of journalists go unpunished.”

India has the unenvious distinction of being among countries where oligarchs take control of major media outlets with their money power and put them at the service of the ruling dispensation. The report says “the conglomerate led by Indian entrepreneur Gautam Adani” is in the same brackets with Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan who seek to criminalise journalism via abusive legal proceedings against media outlets and journalists. India, like many other countries, witnesses how Press freedom is gravely suppressed by those who strive every day to undermine the credibility of media by exploiting the opportunities to repress journalism by creating a situation whereby the media sees imminent economic collapse if it exposes misdeeds of authorities. The report also notes how in India and elsewhere public hatred is fuelled through digital attacks on independent journalism, orchestrated or supported by those in power. In Argentina, President Javier Milei infamously coined the slogan, “we don’t hate journalists enough.” He uses this strategy at the highest level of the state. According to the RSF findings, he published over 1,600 posts on his X account that were hostile to the Press in just 47 days, between April and May 2026.

The irony of the situation is that high quality journalism has never been more necessary than now when strife and conflict are rising, AI slop and malicious fabrications spreading on platforms run by big tech firms are posing grave threat to democracy, freedom of speech and expression and truth is becoming the biggest casualty. To make matters worse the US, which previously acted as the savior in cases of threatened journalists overseas, sometimes helping to ease their conditions, is now led by a man who has called news media “the enemy of the American people.” US President Donald Trump is currently pursuing a lawsuit of $10 billion against the BBC. He has also sought to dismantle federally funded organisations which were an important source of independent reporting on many repressive nations.

Still not all is lost. The silver lining is becoming visible. An appeals court panel in the USA recently ruled that the administration had illegally fired the head of Voice of America. In these gloomy times the youths and democracy-loving people across the globe, including India, are coming forward in a manner that may stop the dictators and autocrats in their tracks. Recent elections in Serbia, Brazil and the US and the emergence of bloggers and media platforms working on a shoe-string budget in India are evidence that journalism, alongside activism, can be a bulwark against attacks on Press freedom and democracy.

news.title: 10,000+ flights hit by disruption as US air-traffic system remains crippled
news.text: US flyers had to face another day of long waits and disrupted travel on Sunday, as more than 10,000 flights remained cancelled or delayed for the third day in a row.While airlines raced to get their schedules back on track, transportation secretary Sean Duffy said that things could return to normal by Monday (local time).The disruption began after a router replacement triggered a chain of technical problems across air traffic control centres. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is yet to identify the exact cause, even as the incident has renewed concerns about ageing technology and the need to upgrade the country's air traffic systems.The disruption continued to affect airlines across the country on Sunday. According to aviation data site FlightAware, more than 2,300 flights were cancelled and around 7,700 delayed.Saturday was even worse, with airlines cancelling more than 6,400 flights and reporting over 8,000 delays, according to Reuters.JetBlue saw the highest cancellations on Sunday, with 28% of its flights affected. American Airlines cancelled 17% of its flights, while United Airlines, Southwest and Delta reported cancellations of 3% to 5%.Speaking on ABC, Duffy said that flights would come "back to normal" on Sunday "but probably fully normal" on Monday. He also stressed that keeping passengers safe remained the FAA's priority.One router, a chain of problems: What went wrongThe trouble started with maintenance work involving routers used by the FAA. According to officials, the installation of at least one new router by FAA contractor L3Harris at a remote facility led to a huge flow of data at other air traffic control centres, affecting their communication systems.Duffy said the replacement of a router at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas. The Amarillo router began broadcasting, causing other routers at air traffic control centres across the country to become overloaded.The FAA said on Sunday that it had disabled the "functionality of the originating routers". It also took the same step for around 60 similar routers used in the air traffic control system.However, the exact reason behind the failure remains unclear. Duffy said the maintenance work had been carried out thousands of times in the past without any problems.The worker who installed the router was not suspected of deliberately causing the disruption.The worker was "a good American patriot, we believe, a veteran — so we don't think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install," Duffy said. "But we don't actually have the root cause."Duffy also said the routers that experienced problems were bought in 2001 and had become outdated by 2006.FAA still has no clear answerThe technical failure led the FAA to issue a nationwide ground stop on Friday, bringing nearly all departing flights to a halt for almost five hours.It was the longest nationwide halt to US air travel since the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda attacks on the United States.Duffy said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or any other deliberate attempt to disrupt the system. However, the FAA is still trying to establish what caused the failure.The incident has once again highlighted the challenges facing the US air traffic control system. It has been struggling with ageing technology, equipment and communication problems, along with a shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers.The flight disruptions have added urgency to the debate over modernising the country's air traffic control system.Duffy has called for $50 billion in funding to upgrade the infrastructure, raising his earlier demand of $30 billion. This is in addition to the $12.5 billion approved by Congress last year.US President Donald Trump also called for more funding on Sunday, making his first public comments on the weekend's air travel disruptions."We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," Trump wrote on social media. "Congress must approve."But the demand for more money has not gone unchallenged. US Representatives Rick Larsen and André Carson, the top Democrats on the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and its aviation subcommittee, respectively, questioned why additional funds were needed.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.
news.summary: US airlines faced significant disruptions as more than 10,000 flights were canceled or delayed due to technical failures. The issues resulted from maintenance work on routers used by the Federal Aviation Administration, leading to widespread communication problems. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated that the situation could normalize by Monday, highlighting ongoing challenges with aging technology.

news.title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions  - Puerto Rico Tribune – Daily
news.text:
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.

It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given.

More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded.

Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working, and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies.

As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays.

But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented.

While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind.

Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades.

“Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday.

“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.”

Spotlight on a defence contractor

Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday.

But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines.

A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network.

In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris.

“Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said.

Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.”

L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.

It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems.

But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation.

In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation.

“The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained.

“As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.”

In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics.

“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.

Ageing FAA infrastructure

Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure.

The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear.

Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.

In a September report, the Government Accountability Office, an independent agency tasked with reviewing government departments, highlighted a series of areas in dire need of upgrades.

Computers used by air traffic controllers to display key information like flight approach paths and aviation warnings were using obsolete hardware, including screens from the 1980s and floppy disk drives.

Thousands of radios and specialised switches that allow radio communication over phone lines also rely on obsolete technology that is no longer manufactured.

The agency had been forced to look for replacement parts on the online marketplace eBay, according to Duffy.

The Government Accountability Office also pointed to the continued use of paper flight strips, slips of paper printed for each flight coming into an air traffic controller’s area of responsibility.

Those documents help decide how to coordinate movements like takeoffs and landings so planes do not collide. But the print-out system has already caused dangerous situations.

In August 2023, for instance, a printer used to print flight strips at San Diego International airport jammed. As air traffic controllers tried to fix it, a Southwest Airlines aircraft almost hit a Cessna jet by about 30 metres (100 feet).

Before Friday’s incident, the last national ground stop happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) system stopped working.

Built in 1985, the NOTAM system was responsible for sending emergency messages out about dangerous weather, congestion or other safety issues.

Its failure prompted the FAA to undertake a major review. The Government Accountability Office ultimately found that, out of the 138 systems the FAA relied on, 51 were unsustainable, and another 54 were potentially unsustainable because of ageing technology.

Fifty-eight of those systems, according to the accountability office, had a critical impact on the safety of air traffic in the US.

Unmet upgrades and lack of oversight

In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA had failed to meet at least four of its 11 recommendations for modernising air traffic systems.

One reason for the failure was the complexity of the upgrades. The FAA reportedly has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda, and it has struggled to coordinate the repairs, leaving it unable to prepare for network-wide problems.

The accountability office also determined that the FAA failed to make upgrades because it was not properly overseeing work done by its contractors.

It also pointed to a lack of funding. Unlike many critical government agencies, the FAA’s budget is not mandated by law, so Congress has to approve spending for the agency each year.

Even if Congress does allocate funding, the Trump administration does not have to use all of the money right away, and Democrats have pointed to unspent funds as part of the problem.

Though Congress allocated $12.5bn for the FAA’s upgrades in 2025, the Trump administration has only committed to spending $4bn of that sum. Only approximately $1bn has been spent so far.

Still, Duffy has argued that the FAA needs at least $50bn in the wake of Friday’s grounding.

Democrats like DeLauro have called that sum a “ransom without a real plan to deliver”. She urged full transparency from Duffy and the FAA.

“No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight,” she said.

news.title: India joins US-led pact to secure AI supply chains, critical technologies amid China rivalry: Report
news.text:
ANIIndia has joined a US-led agreement to protect critical technologies and AI supply chains through greater cooperation among partner nations as Washington seeks to counter China's growing influence in strategic sectors. 

Washington DC: India has joined the US and several other nations in signing the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, a move aimed at safeguarding critical technologies and AI supply chains amid intensifying competition with China, the Financial Times reported.According to the Financial Times, US Under-Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said that India, along with South Korea, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, had signed the declaration, while Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission were expected to sign it the following week.The agreement, signed by the US and its partners, including Japan, Australia, Israel and the United Kingdom, seeks to establish a joint list of critical technologies and supply chains underpinning AI that require greater protection.The initiative is part of Pax Silica, a US-led effort to strengthen AI-related supply chains, spanning semiconductors, critical minerals, energy and advanced manufacturing, as Washington and its partners seek to enhance cooperation amid increasing competition and economic pressure from China.Explaining the significance of the agreement, Helberg told the Financial Times that AI supply chains are spread across multiple countries, making international cooperation essential for their security.Live Events"The know how to design a chip, the machine that makes it and the port that ships it can all be in different countries," Helberg said."What makes the San Francisco Declaration historic is that Pax Silica partners have agreed to treat the security of those technologies and the infrastructure behind them as a shared responsibility," he added.Launched in December 2025 by Helberg, Pax Silica is the US State Department's flagship initiative focused on AI and supply-chain security. It aims to develop cooperation among partner countries across critical minerals, energy inputs, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors and AI infrastructure.The initiative has also expanded its membership, with Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, El Salvador, the European Union, Germany, Greece, Kazakhstan, the Netherlands and Panama joining the Pax Silica Declaration at the 2026 Summit.The additions brought the number of signatories to 24, including Australia, Finland, India, Israel, Japan, Norway, Qatar, South Korea, Singapore, Sweden, the Philippines, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom.The latest development comes amid expanding India-US cooperation on critical technologies and trusted infrastructure.Earlier this month, foreign ministers of the Quad grouping - India, the United States, Japan and Australia - announced plans to provide more than USD 85 million in technical and financial assistance to broaden regional access to trusted AI infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific.The announcement was made following a meeting of the four countries' foreign ministers on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Summit in Georgia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong attended the meeting.Washington also announced a separate USD 10 million allocation to support critical minerals recycling initiatives in India and ASEAN member states.The agreement comes as US President Donald Trump prepares to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.text: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will travel to Manila on Monday for a two-day visit to attend the 23rd India-Asean Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit. Maritime security, regional stability and expanding trade ties are expected to be key focus areas at the meetings.Announcing his visit to Manila, PM Modi said in a post on X, "Will be in Manila, Philippines later today and tomorrow to attend the following programmes: 23rd Asean-India Summit. 21st East Asia Summit.""India attaches immense importance to close friendship with Asean nations. I’m also looking forward to interacting with the Indian community based in the Philippines," he added.The visit comes as India seeks to strengthen its strategic engagement with Southeast Asia amid rapid geopolitical changes in the Indo-Pacific. The Philippines, which is chairing the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) this year, is hosting both summits.According to the ministry of external affairs (MEA), Prime Minister will attend a dinner hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on November 16 before participating in the India-Asean Summit and the East Asia Summit process on November 17.Bilateral meetings with other leaders are also being planned.Speaking at a special briefing, MEA secretary (East) Rudrendra Tandon said India's engagement with Asean, both as a regional grouping and with individual member countries, was an important part of its Act East policy."We strongly believe that as an Indian Ocean country that abuts this very important Southeast Asian maritime zone, a strong strategic relationship with the Asean member states, as a collective as well as individually, is good for both of us," Tandon said.Maritime security, regional stability in focusMaritime cooperation is expected to feature prominently in the discussions, particularly as India and Asean share adjoining maritime zones and face common regional security challenges.India and Asean marked 2026 as the Year of Maritime Cooperation, with several activities aimed at highlighting their shared maritime interests.New Delhi believes closer strategic cooperation with Southeast Asian countries will help both sides deal with changing geopolitical developments and contribute to peace and stability across Asia.The East Asia Summit, an Asean-led forum involving regional and major global powers, will provide another platform for leaders to discuss international security issues and matters of common concern.This year's summit process is being held under the theme "navigating the future", with leaders expected to focus on strengthening cooperation and building resilience amid global uncertainties.Trade ties and AITIGA reviewEconomic cooperation will also be an important part of India's engagement with Asean.Bilateral trade between India and the regional bloc stands at around $122 billion, making Asean one of India's major trading partners.India is also pushing for an early conclusion to the ongoing review of the India-Asean Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA), which New Delhi hopes will help address trade imbalances and improve market access.Tandon said discussions on the review were continuing, while acknowledging that negotiations involving multiple countries take time.BrahMos, South China Sea and MyanmarDefence cooperation between India and Asean countries has also gained momentum in recent years.The Philippines became India's first foreign customer for the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile in 2022, signing a $375-million deal for three shore-based anti-ship missile batteries.Philippine defence secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr recently indicated that Manila was interested in acquiring additional systems and had submitted a wish list to India.On the South China Sea, India has maintained that any Asean-China Code of Conduct should be consistent with international law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).The situation in Myanmar is another issue likely to feature in regional discussions. India has opposed diplomatic isolation of Myanmar, citing its geographical proximity, shared 1,643-km border and major connectivity projects, including the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project.Myanmar is expected to be represented in Manila by a foreign ministry official.Quad summit, possible PM Modi-Trump meetingThe Manila visit has also drawn attention amid discussions around a possible Quad leaders' summit involving India, the US, Japan and Australia.US secretary of state Marco Rubio had indicated last month that the Quad summit was planned alongside the wider meetings in the Philippines. However, the MEA said it had no confirmed information on the meeting or a possible interaction between PM Modi and US President Donald Trump.A meeting between PM Modi and Trump, if scheduled, would come amid ongoing India-US trade negotiations and following recent setbacks for the Republican Party in the US midterm elections.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

news.title: Brent Crude Holds Near $95/Barrel As Fresh US-Iran Flare Ups Dim Growing Supply Surplus
news.text: Brent crude prices stabilised around $95.4 per barrel levels on Monday after a two-week decline as fresh attacks between the United States and Iran overshadowed signs of a well-supplied physical market. The West Texas Intermediate (WTI) traded 0.32% lower at $88.28 per barrel. On Sunday, Iran targeted a US helicopter base in Bahrain after weeks of not attacking the Persian Gulf. Meanwhile, Iranian media reported that five tankers caught fire after being struck by mines in the last 48 hours, without identifying them. news.title: Nigerian passengers stranded as US flight disruptions persist
news.text:
Travel plans of hundreds of Nigerian travellers have been disrupted following widespread flight cancellations in the United States triggered by a nationwide air traffic control ground stop since Friday.

 The disruption, which affected thousands of flights across the US, has continued to take a toll on international aviation operations, leaving passengers travelling from Nigeria to the US, as well as those scheduled to return to Nigeria, grappling with delays, cancellations and uncertainty.

Findings by The PUNCH showed that several Nigerian passengers scheduled to travel to the US over the weekend were unable to embark on their journeys as planned, with some having to abandon their trips temporarily or postpone their flights until airlines could restore normal operations.

 Some perssengers temporarily spent hours within the airport terminal while some others checked into a hotel around the airport with the thought that the disruptions would only last for a day.

A passenger, Sola Aina, who spoke with our correspondent on Sunday, said he had been forced to return home after spending days waiting for his flight to be rescheduled.

 “I just have to return home today. I have come for a Friday flight before we heard of the troubles in the U.S, I have to sleep in a hotel since Friday believing that the issues would be sorted before Sunday night, but this is almost 7:00pm again now.

 “I have ordered a cab. I have to return to Ibadan. It’s very painful but I don’t have an option,” he said.

Another passenger, Faruq Akinwale, said the disruption had affected his plans to return home urgently, as his wife and sick child were in the US.

 “I have a sick child with my wife in the U.S and I need to return home urgently, but what do I do? But I understand that no one can be blamed for this, but I will only appeal that everyone concerned should please hasten up whatever they are doing, I pray God help them,” he said.

 A mother of two, Mrs Aderemi, also expressed disappointment over the situation, saying she and her family had been left with little choice but to return home.

 “We will just return home, the situation is just understandable even though it’s painful,” she said.

 Similarly, another passenger, Charles Adekunle, said the disruption had affected his travel plans, although he did not disclose whether he intended to reschedule his trip.

 The situation has also affected passengers travelling from the US to Nigeria, particularly those booked on international services connecting major American cities to Lagos and Abuja.

 Airlines operating flights between Nigeria and the US, either directly or through connecting routes, include Qatar Airways, Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines, Emirates, Virgin Atlantic and British Airways, among others.

 Although the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the nationwide ground stop on Saturday evening, airlines have continued to battle operational challenges, including the repositioning of aircraft and flight crews displaced by the disruption. 

 An update published on Delta Air Lines’ website on Saturday indicated that the carrier was still working to restore normal operations following the FAA-mandated ground stop, which lasted more than four hours.

 The airline said passengers scheduled to travel between 13 and 15 November, 2026, could change their bookings without paying additional charges.

 It also encouraged customers with flexible travel arrangements to move their flights to Monday, 16 November, or later, warning that passengers travelling over the weekend should expect delays and further schedule adjustments.

 Delta said, “Delta continues to restore operations following an FAA-mandated nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, November 13. Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft.

 “Taking care of customers remains our focus, and we continue to offer flexible rebooking options to change flights at no extra cost. Customers who have flexible travel plans are encouraged to move their flights to Monday, Nov. 16 or later.

 “If you are traveling on Saturday, please allow extra time and check the Delta app or delta.com for the latest flight status and travel information. Delta will provide customers with as much notice as possible about changes to flight schedules. When a cancellation does occur, Delta will automatically rebook customers to the next best itinerary.”

 Meanwhile, the Donald Trump administration has warned that disruptions to air travel across the United States could persist until Monday, extending the wait for a full return to normal operations.

 Hundreds more flights were cancelled on Sunday, raising concerns about the scale of the disruption in the world’s largest economy, which has one of the busiest aviation networks globally.

 US officials attributed Friday’s disruption to faulty work carried out during an upgrade of air traffic control communication cables.

 President Donald Trump broke his silence on the crisis on Sunday, blaming the previous administration of Joe Biden for the state of the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.

 The FAA chief, Bryan Bedford, had said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans affected by the disruption would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.

 However, Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, said on Sunday that the restoration of normal operations would take longer because aircraft and flight crews had been displaced during the disruption.
news.summary:
Hundreds of Nigerian travellers are stranded due to widespread US flight disruptions caused by a nationwide air traffic control ground stop.

news.title: Thousands of U.S. flights canceled, delayed for third day in a row
news.text:
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK >> U.S. air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normalcy by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

More than 2,300 flights nationwide were canceled and some 7,700 were delayed on Sunday, according to aviation data site FlightAware. Airlines on Saturday had canceled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000.

Duffy said on ABC’s “This Week” program that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other malicious intent in the matter, but the cause remained unclear. Duffy said that flights would come “back to normal” on Sunday “but probably fully normal” on Monday, and emphasized the Federal Aviation Administration’s focus on keeping passengers safe.

On Sunday, 28% of JetBlue flights and 17% of American Airlines flights were canceled, with United Airlines, Southwest and Delta reporting cancellations of 3% to 5% of their flights.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to US air travel since the September 11, 2001, al Qaeda attacks on the United States.

The installation by FAA contractor L3Harris of at least one new router at a remote facility led to a situation in which other air traffic control centers were overloaded with a flood of data that hampered communications systems, according to officials.

Duffy said on Sunday that the replacement of a router at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, triggered problems with a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, which started broadcasting and overloading routers at other air traffic control centers across the country.

The “functionality of the originating routers” has been disabled, the FAA said on Sunday, adding that it did the same for about 60 similar routers in the air traffic control system. But the FAA still does not know what ultimately caused the problem that occurred with maintenance work that had been done thousands of times before without issue, Duffy said.

The worker who installed the router was “a good American patriot, we believe, a veteran — so we don’t think that someone tried to sabotage the network on the install,” Duffy said. “But we don’t actually have the root cause.”

Friday’s disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

The routers that experienced issues were purchased in 2001 and were obsolete by 2006, Duffy said. Since Friday, Duffy has called for $50 billion in funding to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of $30 billion — after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year.

More spending sought

President Donald Trump on Sunday made his first public comments on this weekend’s air travel issues, also calling for additional funding from US lawmakers.

“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs,” Trump wrote on social media. “Congress must approve.”

Democrats are set to take control of Congress from Trump’s fellow Republicans in January following their gains in the November 3 US midterm elections.

Duffy’s plea for more money drew skepticism from US Representatives Rick Larsen and André Carson, the top Democrats on the House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and its aviation subcommittee, respectively.

Of the $12.5 billion approved in 2025 for upgrades to the air traffic control system, about $11 billion remains unspent, Larsen and Carson said in a statement on Saturday.

“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” Larsen and Carson asked in their statement.

Duffy on Sunday said that the money allocated last year was earmarked only for certain spending, and did not include funds for new software to manage the airspace.

Air travel observers have also called for increased spending by private investors.

“We can’t rely only on government investments. … You have to have private investment,” said Justin Erbacci, director general of the Airports Council International (ACI) global trade group.

Erbacci, speaking at a Montreal aviation infrastructure forum on Sunday, did not mention Friday’s ground stop, but he said that investment must be made in air transport to accommodate rising traffic and outdated systems.

Global air passenger traffic is projected to more than double by 2050, according to data from airline trade group IATA.
news.summary: WASHINGTON/NEW YORK >> U.S. air travel disruptions continued for a third day with more than 10,000 flights affected on Sunday, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy predicted a return to normalcy by Monday even as airlines scrambled to get back on schedule following a systemwide ground stop.

news.title: The driverless taxis, robots and tech companies in APEC host city Shenzhen show China's ambitions
news.text:
The app showed one minute until the taxi’s arrival. Not far from the pickup spot, the blue and white SUV with a small robot graphic on its sides approached through the light traffic. It looked like any other car, except that no one was behind the wheel.

Welcome to Shenzhen, a hub of technological development in China, where some of the latest advancements are taking shape, from artificial intelligence and robotics to electric and autonomous vehicles.

While some of these innovations can now be seen in other Chinese cities, Shenzhen has long been considered one of the country’s leading technology centers and is home to some of its best-known companies, like the telecommunication firm Huawei, electric vehicle maker BYD and internet and gaming giant Tencent.

The city will draw more attention as it hosts this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Chinese President Xi Jinping will welcome representatives from APEC’s 21 members, including U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia’s leader Vladimir Putin.

The gathering comes as China and the U.S. compete for leadership in technologies such as artificial intelligence in a rivalry intertwined with disputes over tariffs and access to critical minerals, and as a trade truce was recently extended until January.

Shenzhen’s transformation from a testing ground for market-oriented reforms into a tech center reflects China’s rise as a global economic competitor.

“Shenzhen is one of the most important symbols of China’s reform and opening up through its strong global role in trade, manufacturing, and innovation,” said Gary Ng, senior economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.

 From a fishing town to a special economic zone 

The city's transformation date to 1980, when China was opening up its economy. Then-leader Deng Xiaoping declared the former fishing village as one of China's first special economic zones, where the Communist Party would allow free enterprise. That opened the door to foreign investment and manufacturing for export until it also became a place for companies to develop their own technologies.

Shenzhen is now a metropolis of more than 18 million people. From the observation deck of China’s second-tallest building, the 600-meter (1,968-feet) Ping An tower, people can see a city of glass towers amid green spaces, with mountains rising through parts of it.

This is a city known as a place to see driverless taxis, robots and electric vehicles, though some of the technologies aren't visible everywhere. 

Drone deliveries only serve specific locations, while driverless taxis or robotaxis begin at designated pickup spots on the western side of the city. And some restrictions were imposed ahead of the APEC summit, being held Wednesday and Thursday. Drone deliveries were suspended, and robotaxi services were reduced.

 A ride without a driver 

Pony.ai is one of the companies providing driverless taxis, with a fleet of almost 2,000 SUVs painted in blue and white, the image of a small robot named “Popo” on their sides. Founded in 2016, the company operates in Shenzhen and three other Chinese cities: Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou.

But the robotaxis cannot go anywhere you want. Trips are limited to designated pickup and drop-off points within approved service areas.

One of the few places where passengers could take a robotaxi a week before the summit was in front of Tencent, the company behind the messaging and payment app WeChat.

Three AP journalists took a trip to one of the available destinations, a hotel 7.6 kilometers (4.7 miles) away. 

The app warned that passengers had less than 60 seconds to get in. Once inside the car, an Arcfox, a screen displayed “Popo” giving safety instructions and asking customers to fasten their seatbelts.

For 24 minutes, the car crossed several streets, slowing down at corners and stopping completely for people and red lights. Near a corner where it needed to turn left, it switched on its turn signal and waited. When the traffic light turned green and traffic began moving, another driver let it through. 

The ride was smooth — and the cost was 12.7 yuan ($1.90), cheaper than a regular taxi because of a first-trip discount.

Cong Lin, Pony.ai's public affairs director, said the cars use 34 sensors and are able to perceive 360 degrees with a range of up to 615 meters (about 2,018 feet). The robotaxis averaged about 23 and 25 trips each day in February, she said.

Does the company envision a day when all taxis in Shenzhen are driverless? “We don’t see robot taxis as a replacement for regular cars or regular taxis,” Lin said. “We see ourselves as just one more option for the riders to choose from.”

 Companies say Shenzhen offers policy support and suppliers at hand 

When China marked 40 years of Shenzhen as special economic zone, in 2020, Xi described the city as “a miracle in the world development history.”

Government support is among the factors that have helped shape its growth and attracted migrants and entrepreneurs from other cities.

“The more flexible and open government policies have enabled experimentation different from the rest of China. At the same time, the proximity to Hong Kong is important for attracting capital, developing commercial expertise, and accessing world markets,” said Ng, from Natixis.

Cong, from Pony.ai, said Shenzhen offers “policy clarity (and) government support, so there’s a very clear pathway for autonomous driving companies like us to follow, from the testing with a safety operator on board to a commercial service with a safety operator on board to fully driverless.”

Shenzhen is also home to Pudu robotics, which makes service robots that deliver meals in restaurants, clean floors and guide shoppers to products. The company, founded here in 2016, develops humanoid robots and wheeled robots with arms, focusing on specific tasks such as picking up and delivering items in office buildings and packing goods in warehouses.

Guo Cong, chief technology officer and co-founder of Pudu, said the city provides what the company needs, from suppliers of hardware and mechanical parts to software and businesses putting their robots to work. 

He added that supply chain support can arrive within half a day, while customers are close so engineers can visit within an hour or two.

“Shenzhen shows Chinese speed, and also shows Chinese strategy for efficiency and innovation to the global world,” he said. “Shenzhen is a pioneer part of China that really shows this kind of spirit to the world.”

 A city that keeps drawing new people 

People from across China have been moving to Shenzhen for decades. While some neighborhoods resemble other Chinese cities, some residents see it as a place with a distinctive energy.

“My impression of Shenzhen is that it’s a vibrant, youthful city, and its residents are well-mannered,” said Zhong Luqin, a kindergarten teacher who moved to Shenzhen from Zhanjiang, another city in Guangdong province.

“There is a broadly-used comment to describe Shenzhen: ‘workers with a hustle mentality’,” she added minutes after taking a selfie with an APEC summit sign in the background. “It captures the city’s very fast pace of life.”

Associated Press video producer Olivia Zhang and writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report.
news.summary: APEC host city Shenzhen is a window into China’s technological ambitions and economic transformation
news.author: E. Eduardo Castillo

news.title: Trump administration asks for billions to overhaul FAA. Democrats question how money was spent
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The Trump administration is pressing for $50 billion to address an aging air traffic control system after problems with routers apparently led to a rare nationwide grounding of all planes, but Democrats are demanding answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared.

The growing rift over how to address the Federal Aviation Administration’s vulnerabilities comes as passengers across the country are struggling to get to where they need to go after thousands of flights were grounded Friday, and investigators are still trying to figure out what went wrong.

President Donald Trump, who hadn’t spoken publicly or commented on the flight grounding, finally weighed in Sunday with comments on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and calling for more money to pay for improvements to the system.

The finger-pointing and blame-shifting between the Republican administration and Democrats in Congress underscored the political division that could only grow wider when Democrats take control in January and scrutiny of the Trump administration accelerates, even on a matter that impacts all travelers.

During appearances on Sunday morning talk shows, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy detailed what is known — and still unclear — about the problems that led up to his decision Friday to ground the planes, as he also pushed Congress for billions more to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.

Duffy details what happened

In a post on X, Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.

After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Arkansas, and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop.

The FAA said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said. The contractor blocked the two locations in Arkansas and Texas, and the agency said that stabilized the network.

Duffy said billions are needed to build a “brand new architecture” for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it “tomorrow” if the money is there.

Aging air traffic control system has been a problem for years

The need to upgrade the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years.

Under President Joe Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airports for such things as new runways and taxiways, and new and refurbished terminals.

Under Trump, a Republican-led Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.

The administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.

In a hearing on Sept. 15, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said with the money Congress provided, “we are executing on the most ambitious modernization and delivering it in record time.”

The FAA upgrade has two phases. The first, funded by the $12.5 billion, is supposed to be completed by December 2028. A second phase involves developing new systems to track aircraft and optimize traffic. Bedford told lawmakers in September that the second phase will cost at least an additional $10 billion.

Separately, Sen. Eric Schmitt, a Missouri Republican, in September introduced a bill that builds on the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year and calls for about $30 billion more in new investments in the nation’s air transportation system. Duffy has also pushed for that funding.

Schmitt’s bill would include the $10 billion Bedford said is needed for the second phase. On top of that it includes money to modernize up to three medium hub airports and to make various airport improvements around the country, from new air traffic control towers to new terminals.

Then on Friday Duffy said he wants $50 billion, but he hasn’t detailed what it’s for. He said Saturday that he’ll be sending a detailed request to legislators on Monday.

Democrats question rising costs and why money hasn’t been spent

Congressional Democrats say they also want to upgrade the country’s aging air traffic control system. But they are questioning the price tag.

Democrats on the House Transportation Committee said most of the money appropriated last year remains unspent.

“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking Democrat on the committee, and Rep. André Carson, the top Democrat on a subcommittee with jurisdiction over aviation issues, said in a statement.

Democrats on the House Appropriations Committee are asking the same question. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the panel, said Congress has shown it’s willing to invest in modernizing the FAA.

“But we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner. Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner,” DeLauro said.

Duffy said Sunday the money appropriated last year by Congress will be spent by the end of 2028. He also said his agency was restricted by Congress in how it could be spent and that didn’t include spending on the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.

Trump conspicuously quiet for 2 days

Trump had not commented publicly or on social media after the ground stop was ordered Friday afternoon, although he was active on social media about unrelated matters.

Sunday morning, he weighed in with a post on Truth Social, saying his administration has begun upgrading the air traffic control system but it should not be done in “drips and drabs.”

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old — RIDICULOUS!”

Duffy said Trump has been “fully engaged” on the ground stop.

Travel should return to normal by Monday

As for the traveling public, Duffy said that “as we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity.”

Duffy said the administration feels “pretty good” that the breakdown did not result from a hacking event. He said various intelligence agencies have said they were not finding the “chatter or the footprints that we would normally see if this was a cyberattack.”

Duffy appeared on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” CNN’s “State of the Union,” “Fox News Sunday,” NBC’s “Meet the Press” and ABC’s “This Week.”
news.summary: The Trump administration is requesting $50 billion to modernize the aging FAA air traffic control system following a nationwide flight grounding due to technical issues. While Republicans cite the need for improvements, Democrats are demanding accountability regarding previously allocated funds and questioning the steep increase in the funding request.

news.title: US-bound migrant caravan departs Honduras despite Trump warnings
news.text:
SAN PEDRO SULA, Honduras: A new caravan of more than 100 migrants set off on foot from Honduras toward the United States on Sunday, an AFP journalist observed.

The group was seen carrying backpacks and water for the long journey, despite warnings from US President Donald Trump to stay away.

The migrants, some carrying children in their arms, left the bus terminal in San Pedro Sula, in the north of the Central American country, shortly before 4:00 p.m. (2100 GMT). They aim to reach Corinto, on the border with Guatemala.

“We’re going with the intention of working,” Alexander Vallecillo, an 18-year-old bricklayer who is leaving his wife and eight-month-old son behind in Honduras, told AFP.

“With the situation here, you can’t get ahead,” Vallecillo lamented.

The caravan’s final destination is the United States, even as Trump, who lost control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, maintains a crackdown on irregular migration.

Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it fails to stop the migrants.

The US embassy in Tegucigalpa has also warned that caravans that “cross illegally” will face legal consequences.

“The laws did not change after the November 3 elections,” it posted on X.

“That man [Trump] is a bad person. We hope the results [of the congressional elections] will help us a little,” Vallecillo said.

Another caravan of around 1,000 Central Americans reached Mexico in early November, while a separate group of around 100 migrants was dispersed by Mexican authorities this month.

On Friday, following Trump’s tariff threat, President Claudia Sheinbaum said there were “no more caravans” of migrants traveling through Mexico toward its northern neighbor.

According to Sheinbaum, Mexico has broken up 24 caravans since Trump’s return to power in 2024.

Estela Rodriguez, the mother of two girls, aged two and five, said she decided to migrate after a criminal organization tried to extort money from her cake business.

The situation in the United States “is complicated,” but “it’s worse here, and you have a family to support,” Rodriguez, a 20-year-old businesswoman who is also traveling alone, told AFP.

news.text: SAN FRANCISCO, United States — US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia Sunday to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.Speaking on 'Fox News Sunday Morning Futures' three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China.The United States forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorize sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese -- but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.'Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,' Bessent said.'What's more important here,' he said, 'is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.'He alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company that Huang's alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for.'And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?'Of Alice Huang he said: 'It doesn't matter to me whether she's a spy or not. Ives also said that China is likely celebrating Huang's departure from Nvidia because it "narrows the gap" between the country and the U.S.

"He's worth about $1 trillion in the valuation of Nvidia, and that's a huge reason the stock's been down," Ives said. "Obviously, part of the issue when it comes to Trump ... he was showcased.
