news.title: 'Not Cuba or Venezuela': Iran warns it will not wait for US attack before responding
news.text: Iran has warned that it will not wait for the United States to launch an attack before responding, with deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi accusing Washington of potentially using diplomacy to buy time for another military operation.Speaking to Iranian state television in an interview carried by Fars news agency, Gharibabadi said Tehran was preparing for three possible scenarios in its dealings with Washington: diplomacy, an economic blockade and military aggression.“Iran is not Cuba that you can blockade, nor is it Venezuela that you can force to surrender,” he said, adding that US forces had so far failed to achieve success through either an air or land blockade. He also claimed that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was producing missiles with “new ranges”.Gharibabadi suggested that Washington could be exploiting diplomatic engagement to prepare the ground for another attack. He also said Iran remained in a state of war, rejecting the description of the current situation as “neither war nor peace”.“My personal belief is that from a legal perspective, we are still in a state of war and not in a neither-war-nor-peace situation,” he said.Tehran sets conditions for IAEA access to nuclear sitesGharibabadi said the IRGC would not allow the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to inspect Iran's nuclear facilities until Tehran's conditions were met and the war had permanently ended.The remarks came after the UN nuclear watchdog called on Iran to restore access for inspectors to its nuclear facilities, including sites damaged during the conflict.“The agency’s request to visit Iran’s damaged nuclear sites is likely an assessment of the effectiveness of American weaponry,” Gharibabadi said.The deputy foreign minister, who previously served as Iran's ambassador to the IAEA, said Washington would first have to provide guarantees that Iran's conditions would be respected.“First and foremost, the US must provide the necessary guarantees that all of Iran’s conditions will be observed,” he said.Iran outlines demands for diplomatic agreementIn a separate televised interview with IRNA, Gharibabadi said the United States had repeatedly undermined Tehran's trust in diplomatic negotiations.“The US has shown its bad faith at least three times over the past year and a half. This shows that the US cannot be trusted at the diplomacy table,” he said.He cited the 12-day war and the 40-day war, which he said had taken place while negotiations were under way, as well as a 14-point memorandum of understanding that lasted less than two weeks.Iran's conditions for an agreement include a permanent end to the war on all fronts, the lifting of the US economic blockade and certain sanctions, including those targeting the oil sector, and a resolution of the issue of Iranian assets frozen abroad. Tehran also wants Washington to address the new military equipment and forces deployed in the region after the previous understanding.Gharibabadi said Iran had proposed a seven-day timeline for ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which was subsequently reduced to two days following consultations with mediators over the past two months.“This means the measures could be carried out within two days and ultimately lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that the proposal remained on the table.However, he said differences over the implementation of commitments continued to prevent an agreement. He maintained that the US would have to rebuild Tehran's trust if it wanted to pursue diplomacy.US carrier arrives in Middle East as regional tensions continueMeanwhile, the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, a US official cited by Al Jazeera claimed. It joins two other American carriers already operating within the US Central Command area of responsibility.Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early on Sunday that it had struck a radar system at an American helicopter base in Bahrain, according to state-run IRNA. The US military's Central Command did not immediately comment on the claim.On Friday, Centcom said it had intercepted two Iranian drones heading towards Bahrain and denied an earlier Iranian claim that its forces had struck a US early-warning radar system there.Bahrain's military said on Sunday that its air defence systems had intercepted several Iranian projectiles before they reached their targets.Gharibabadi also criticised Washington's maximum-pressure sanctions policy, describing it as a failed approach that had not achieved its objectives during US President Donald Trump's first term.He acknowledged that sanctions affected ordinary Iranians but argued that their consequences for the global economy, energy and financial markets, as well as the US itself, were greater.You use AI every day. news.title: On election campaigns and election manifestos
news.text:
Governance should focus on sustainable economic development, improving people’s living conditions day by day. If in doubt, ask President Donald Trump. The global rising cost of living or declining standard of living led, invariably, to demonstrations in countries like Germany and France, while United States citizens used the Mid-Term elections in November to demonstrate their displeasure with President Trump and the Republican Party, with the loss of a majority in both the Senate and House of Representatives. With 55 seats in the Senate, the Democrats gained eight more seats lost by the Republicans. In the House, Democrats won 256 seats to the Republicans’ 169.

 According to available research records, the loss by the Republican Party has been attributed to five main causes, namely soaring cost of living, the unpopular Iran war, a disciplined message from the democrats, unpopularity of President Trump in connection to his policies generally and economic policies in particular, and shifts in the position of Hispanic and black voters as related to Trump’s immigration policy. What matters here is the soaring cost of living, a global phenomenon. The state of an economy, specifically citizens’ economic condition, has a way of helping or destroying candidates participating in elections. The rising cost of living phenomenon is the necklace being worn by every country’s leader today!

 When we talk about the macroeconomic goals every country wants to achieve, price stability is central. It seems to be the central point around which achieving other macroeconomic goals revolves. The macro goals or objectives are full employment of resources, economic growth, price stability, balance of payments equilibrium, equitable income distribution and sustainable development. We need stable prices to achieve full employment, yet we need some moderate inflation to achieve economic growth. If the law of supply is to hold, upward adjustment of prices serves to encourage higher supply. That is, the higher the price, the higher the supply.

 And higher supply means growth. Growth, encouraged by higher prices, makes external trade possible, improving the balance of payments and moving it toward equilibrium. Higher economic growth implies higher national income, for which equitable distribution is essential for peace to reign in the country. Sustainable economic growth moves the economy toward rising employment and incomes or the full-employment goal and eventually results in economic development. While moderate price rises necessarily achieve those stated macroeconomic objectives, the kind of rapid inflation being witnessed today creates a disastrous situation, particularly with respect to citizens’ welfare. The fact that this second wave of inflation came from external shocks provides a lesson in policymaking.

 We witnessed the first wave of inflation when the subsidy on fuel was removed and petroleum prices were deregulated, in addition to the massive devaluation of the naira by about 300 per cent. That was a domestic shock and did require some reforms. External shocks require policy revolution to prevent, in the future, the magnitude of the effects that we are having presently. That is why the current political campaign should centre around economic revolution rather than economic reform. 

 Many African leaders are afraid of using revolution but prefer reforms, the language of the World Bank and IMF. Whereas the economic policies are necessary to take Africa out of the economic doldrum, it finds itself in a revolutionary adjustment. There is a need to overhaul the economic system of production whereby we produce to satisfy the industrial needs of advanced economies. We remain producers of raw materials in human and non-human resources. Our physical products feed industries in the Western world, and human resources are attracted by improved working environments and higher wages and salaries.

 A revolution does not mean chaotic changes like the French Revolution, but drastic, radical, or fundamental changes like the First Industrial Revolution in 18th- and 19th-century Great Britain. The revolution transformed global production, labour, and trade through mechanised factories and steam power. What we require in Nigeria and the whole of Africa is revolutionary production in agriculture, factories or industries generally, whereby we export finished products like the rest of the world. The present campaign for election in Nigeria and the manifestos of principal actors should reflect a revolutionary departure from the present situation.

 Such revolutionary changes will minimise the depth of external shocks that we are witnessing now. Politicians should tell us how many megawatts of electricity will be generated yearly and how they will do it. President Tinubu was promising a growth rate of six per cent per year for the next four years. That is not ambitious. He should be proposing a minimum growth of 10 per cent. China did take over 900 million Chinese out of poverty in three decades by growing at 10 per cent per year for more than a decade. According to the World Bank Poverty and Equity Report, an estimated 496 million Indians moved out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, driven by increased employment opportunities. This was linked to sustained growth of about 10 per cent over the decade. Specific government schemes were credited with the massive decline.

 Every presidential candidate should be specific about what to do with agriculture, education, industry, science and technology and medicine. Manifestos must be clear, just like the campaign. Every specific promise must be backed by data and a timeline. We cannot continue to run Nigeria on handouts to consumers; we must run it on jobs and enhanced productivity. A conducive production environment must be promised and fulfilled. This will include reliable electricity or power infrastructure. Without electricity, neither China nor India would have achieved the feats reported. China has long achieved 100 per cent electricity, while India is almost there, with an achievement of over 90 per cent in the last five years. The Nigerian government, like other African governments, must declare revolutionary development rather than unending reforms and transformation.
news.summary:
Nigerian election campaigns and manifestos must focus on economic revolution, not just reform, to tackle the rising cost of living and ensure development.

news.title: Thousands of US flights still cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
news.text:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.

"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 5,000 flights were delayed and 2,000 cancelled on Sunday.

President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports nationwide.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

In the aftermath, FlightAware reported that 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 were cancelled.

The stoppage left passengers stuck on the tarmac, unable to take off or return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to reach their airline. 

The ground stop also had knock-on effects on schedules worldwide, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.

On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.

Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is to blame, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that lets air traffic controllers and pilots communicate.

The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.

He said on Sunday that the router, a piece of equipment that directs traffic across the network, was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".

Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. He said the system needs a complete overhaul.

"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."

In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".

"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.

Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

news.title: Chris Van Hollen Downplays Schumer's Role in Democrats' Midterm Wins
news.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, pushed back Sunday against claims that the New York Democrat deserves significant credit for the party's sweeping midterm victories. The Maryland Democrat argued that the election results reflected voters' rejection of President Donald Trump rather than a successful campaign orchestrated by Democratic leaders in Washington. "This was not a Washington-orchestrated election around the country," Van Hollen said on ABC News' This Week on Sunday. "This was the American people rising up against a lawless president and demanding change." His remarks come as Schumer's allies point to Democrats' historic gains in the Senate as evidence that he deserves another term leading the caucus, setting up a debate over who should receive credit for the party's success—and who should lead it going forward. Newsweek reached out to Schumer's office for comment on Sunday. Why Chris Van Hollen Is Challenging Chuck Schumer Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, securing at least 55 Senate seats after gaining eight. Alaska's Senate race remains uncalled. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, has argued that the results demonstrate the caucus's success under his leadership. "I'm proud of what we've accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said Thursday after Van Hollen announced his challenge. Several prominent Democrats have defended Schumer's record. Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego compared Schumer's leadership to that of a successful sports manager. "When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract," Gallego said. "And this has been a really good election cycle for us." New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who led Senate Democrats' campaign arm this election cycle, also credited Schumer with helping the party win. "He really helped keep the caucus aligned on message and what we were bringing to the American people and helping these candidates deliver," Gillibrand told Vermont television station WCAX. But Van Hollen challenged that interpretation Sunday when ABC's Martha Raddatz cited the World Series analogy again, this time attributing it to Schumer supporter Angus King, the Maine independent who caucuses with Democrats. "I respect the work of the DSCC," Van Hollen said, referring to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. "And I used to chair the DSCC and the DCCC in the House." The DCCC is the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which works to elect Democrats to the House. He then disputed the suggestion that national party leaders had engineered the victories. "We won not just Senate seats and House seats, we won governor's races. We won legislative races," he said. Van Hollen pointed specifically to Senator-elect Scott Colom's victory in Mississippi, arguing that national Democrats had been slow to recognize his potential. "He wasn't recruited or picked by anybody in Washington," Van Hollen said. "And in fact, Washington was very late in the game to supporting that." He also cited Annie Andrews, the Democratic senator-elect from South Carolina, as another example of a victory that he said was not orchestrated by Washington. Newsweek reached out to Gillibrand's office and Colom's campaign for comment on Sunday. Van Hollen Accuses Schumer's Team of Spreading Misinformation Van Hollen went beyond questioning Schumer's role in the election victories, accusing the Democratic leader's team of trying to discourage senators from supporting his challenge. Asked whether he had enough votes to defeat Schumer, Van Hollen said the contest remained open. "I think there's a very open lane here," he said. "The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation. They're essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they're going to support me as a new leader." "But that's part of the problem," he continued. "That's part of the old system." He added: "We just had a great day for our democracy around the country. How about a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus?" Van Hollen did not specify which statements he considered misinformation during the ABC interview. Appearing separately on Fox News Sunday, Van Hollen challenged claims about Schumer's support, accusing his rival's team of putting out inaccurate numbers. "The other team has been putting out numbers that are flatly wrong," he said. "They're trying to create this false sense of momentum." Who Is Supporting Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer? The leadership contest has exposed divisions among Democrats over whether the party should retain its longtime Senate leader or embrace a new direction after its election victories. Van Hollen has secured public endorsements from Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan. "The American people voted for change," Sanders wrote on X Thursday. "They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families." As of Saturday, Schumer had received public endorsements from at least 13 Democratic senators, including Gillibrand, Gallego, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman. Fetterman has gone further, suggesting that Van Hollen's election could become a breaking point in his relationship with the Democratic Party. Asked on Fox News on Saturday whether Van Hollen becoming majority leader would be a red line that could prompt him to leave the party, Fetterman replied: "Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very…hostile to Israel." Other Democrats have called for new leadership without committing to Van Hollen. Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has said Democrats need a new generation of leaders, while Andrews has similarly called for generational change in both parties. The Democratic Socialists of America has also backed a challenge to Schumer, telling Newsweek on Friday that the New York senator had "consistently failed to deliver for the working class." Van Hollen has previously argued that Democrats should welcome debate across the party's ideological spectrum, including from democratic socialists, rather than simply return to the political status quo that preceded Trump's presidency. When Will Democrats Choose Their Senate Majority Leader? Senate Democrats are scheduled to elect their leader on December 1 in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote. A simple majority of the caucus is required to win. Schumer has publicly maintained that he has enough support to remain leader, while Van Hollen said on Fox News Sunday that he had 15 supporters "and growing." The Maryland senator also framed the leadership election on ABC as an opportunity for Democrats to respond to voters' demands for change. "The American people spoke loudly and clearly on Election Day," Van Hollen said. "But they haven't fully hired the Democrats. We have a chance, but we need to earn the people's trust." He added: "I don't think you earn people's trust by simply going back to business as usual, the status quo." Newsweek reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Chris Van Hollen disputes Chuck Schumer's role in Democrats' midterm victories as the rivals compete to lead the Senate majority.
